papers.abstract: Video large language models (Video LLMs) encode each frame into hundreds of visual tokens, making video inference expensive. Existing methods reduce this cost through similarity-based merging or attention-based selection but face two challenges: Hierarchy-blind Pruning, which overlooks regional compressibility and can discard critical evidence, and Attention Drift, where positional effects and attention sinks shift text-to-vision attention away from task relevance. We propose FoveaTree, a two-stage, training-free visual-token pruning framework. First, Merge-Gain Density Estimation measures the feature distortion caused by regional merging and constructs a quadtree-derived density map to guide token dropping, merging, and retention. Second, Attention Tree Pruning uses the surviving units and inherited tree topology to refine text-to-vision attention in intermediate LLM layers, preserving relevant regional evidence while removing low-relevance content. We evaluate FoveaTree on InternVL3.5-8B and Qwen3-VL-8B across five video question-answering benchmarks and one captioning benchmark at 50%, 30%, and 10% visual-token retention. FoveaTree consistently achieves overall state-of-the-art performance across the evaluated settings, offering a strong accuracy-efficiency trade-off.
authors: Zihan Meng
Weidong Chen
Dexiang Hong
Xinyan Liu
Zhendong Mao
bullets: Targets hierarchy-blind pruning and attention drift in Video LLMs.
Estimates regional merge distortion to build a quadtree-based density map for token dropping, merging, and retention.
Refines intermediate-layer text-to-vision attention using surviving tokens and inherited tree structure.
Evaluated on InternVL3.5-8B and Qwen3-VL-8B across five video QA and one captioning benchmark at 50%, 30%, and 10% retention.
Reports consistent overall state-of-the-art performance across evaluated settings, with a strong accuracy-efficiency trade-off.

papers.title: FoveaTree: Information-Density Trees for Query-Guided Visual Token Pruning in Video Large Language Models
papers.tldr: FoveaTree is a training-free, two-stage method that prunes video visual tokens using regional information density and topology-aware attention to reduce inference cost while preserving task-relevant evidence.

papers.abstract: Preference training is the standard recipe for reducing object hallucination in vision-language models, and each new method reports a lower CHAIR score. We ask what that reduction consists of. Every trained system is compared with its base model's caption truncated to the same object recall, which removes the part of the gain that comes from saying less; the remainder is compared with what a deliberately weak, frozen, eleven-feature post-hoc probe fitted on 500 annotated images can reproduce. All criteria were specified in the analysis code and frozen before the outputs they judge existed. For eight public methods on LLaVA-1.5-7B, the probe reproduces at least two thirds of what training removes beyond saying less for 7 of 8 methods on COCO, 8 of 8 on AMBER and 6 of 8 on Object HalBench, with RLAIF-V the consistent exception; a later public method released for both LLaVA-1.5 and Qwen2.5-VL (SENTINEL) meets the same bar on both. On our own DPO checkpoints the accounting holds on Qwen2.5-VL but fails on InternVL2.5 on COCO (2 of 4 training designs). At matched recall, the base model plus the probe beats truncation for 8 of 9 LLaVA-1.5 systems on COCO and 9 of 9 on AMBER, on the two newer backbones, and when realized as actual sentence deletion. The same measure prices training signals: DPO on the model's own samples labelled by the probe or by an object-level CLIP score recovers 0.70 and 0.87 of the beyond-brevity gain of ground-truth-labelled DPO on Qwen2.5-VL (the probe 0.73 on InternVL2.5), both beat length-matched random labels, and CLIP labels buy more than probe labels on COCO. Human judgements show that the sentences the probe deletes are wrong more often than those truncation would delete; a human check of the CHAIR evaluator's precision falls below our pre-set bar, which we report as a limitation.
authors: Lingkai Bu, Qian Gao
bullets: The study separates CHAIR improvements into reduced verbosity versus genuine hallucination reduction by matching object recall with truncated base-model captions.
A frozen, 11-feature probe trained on 500 annotated images reproduces at least two thirds of beyond-brevity gains for most evaluated methods, with RLAIF-V as the main exception.
At matched recall, the base model plus probe generally outperforms truncation across LLaVA-1.5, Qwen2.5-VL, InternVL2.5, COCO, and AMBER evaluations.
Probe- or CLIP-based preference labels recover substantial portions of ground-truth-labelled DPO gains, while outperforming random labels; CLIP labels perform better on COCO.
Human checks support the probe’s deletions, but also identify insufficient precision in the CHAIR evaluator as a limitation.

papers.selection_reason: Investigates 'cheap pruning' techniques in vision-language models (VLMs) to reduce object hallucinations, directly addressing efficiency (token pruning) and VLM robustness.
papers.title: What Does Anti-Hallucination Training Buy? Saying Less, Cheap Pruning, and the Rest
papers.tldr: Much of anti-hallucination training’s apparent benefit comes from shorter captions and can be replicated by a cheap post-hoc probe, though some methods and backbones retain gains beyond brevity.

papers.abstract: Extending multimodal large language models (MLLMs) from images to videos faces substantial memory and latency challenges due to the massive number of visual tokens. These challenges have driven the development of numerous visual token compression methods and more efficient LLM architectures. However, existing compression methods are often evaluated with different training setups, tasks, and models, making fair comparison difficult. Meanwhile, the growing use of hybrid Mamba-Transformer architectures raises questions about whether compression strategies transfer across backbones. We present VidToC, a controlled evaluation framework for representative compression algorithms, LLM backbones, and time encoding strategies, covering training-free and fine-tuned settings on three complementary video understanding tasks. Our results reveal task-dependent compression behavior and characterize the effects of compression placement, time encoding, and backbone choice. These findings provide empirical guidance for designing and selecting video token compression strategies across tasks and training settings.
authors: Zihan Xiao (AIM3 Lab, Renmin University of China), Boshen Xu (AIM3 Lab, Renmin University of China), Pei Fu (MiLM Plus, Xiaomi Inc), Jianzhong Ju (MiLM Plus, Xiaomi Inc), Zhenbo Luo (MiLM Plus, Xiaomi Inc), Jian Luan (MiLM Plus, Xiaomi Inc), Qin Jin (AIM3 Lab, Renmin University of China)
bullets: Video MLLMs face major memory and latency costs from large numbers of visual tokens.
Existing compression methods are difficult to compare fairly because evaluations use different setups, tasks, and models.
VidToC provides a controlled framework spanning representative compression algorithms, LLM backbones, and time-encoding strategies.
Experiments across three video-understanding tasks show that compression behavior depends on the task, compression placement, time encoding, and backbone.
The study offers empirical guidance for selecting compression strategies, including across hybrid Mamba-Transformer architectures.

papers.abstract: Video Large Language Models process large numbers of visual tokens, making token pruning important for efficient inference. Training-free pruning methods differ in whether and how they use the user query, and the value of query conditioning remains unclear. We present a controlled study of training-free, pre-LLM video token selection. Using a shared Qwen-3-VL backbone, token budgets, and decoding settings, we compare 21 pruning principles spanning query-agnostic, shallow query-conditioned, structured query-conditioned, and holistic strategies. To instantiate the last two categories, we introduce Structured Query Pruning, which decomposes the question into semantic anchors, and a Pareto variant, which combines anchor relevance with query-agnostic visual diversity. Across Video-MME, MVBench, and LongVideoBench, relevance computed from the raw question embedding is unreliable (8--16 points below the best methods), whereas anchors derived from query decomposition avoid this failure. However, query access is not inherently advantageous: strong query-agnostic coverage methods remain competitive or superior in the full-field comparison. Relative to a redundancy-only baseline, structured selection helps most on evidence-specific and long-context tasks at tight budgets; on broad tasks, the holistic selector improves over either relevance or redundancy alone. Further, pruning reduces cost and memory. These results support a practical design rule: preserve visual coverage by default, and add structured relevance when the task and token budget demand selective evidence retrieval.
authors: Divya Kothandaraman, Timo Kumkel, Jaclyn Pytlarz
bullets: Compares 21 training-free video token pruning strategies under shared backbone, token budgets, and decoding settings.
Raw question-embedding relevance is unreliable, performing 8–16 points below the best methods across evaluated benchmarks.
Structured query decomposition avoids this failure by selecting tokens linked to semantic anchors.
Query access is not always beneficial: strong coverage-based, query-agnostic methods can match or outperform query-conditioned approaches.
Structured selection helps evidence-specific and long-context tasks at tight budgets; holistic selection helps broad tasks, while pruning reduces cost and memory.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Overview of Structured Query Pruning. Given a user query, the system performs (1) ante-hoc query decomposition to extract semantic anchors (entities, actions) and a task policy, then (2) computes a fused importance score combining intrinsic visual saliency with query-derived semantic relevance. Tokens are ranked and the top-k are retained for LLM generation. The hybrid Pareto strategy jointly optimizes semantic relevance and visual diversity.

papers.abstract: Visual token compression often treats salience or similarity as a proxy for transcription importance. Complete document OCR breaks this assumption: small symbols and repeated entries can be indispensable to the transcript despite being visually inconspicuous. We present Select and Compensate, a two-stage framework built on a simple idea: choosing where to retain a token need not determine all the evidence it carries. Selection combines adaptive encoding resolution with global importance and local contrast to choose which tokens to retain as anchors. Compensation enriches these anchors with nearby discarded content and its relative position, without adding tokens. The OCR backbone remains frozen, and native coordinates and structural tokens are preserved. We evaluate complete page transcription across five backbones on OmniDocBench and document reconstruction on MPDocBench. With half the original visual tokens, our input-adapted configuration reaches 95.42 OmniDocBench Overall on Ovis versus 96.09 for the uncompressed model, and paired evaluations show gains over simply reducing the input resolution on both benchmarks. With the original input grid, our method stays within 0.17 points of the uncompressed model at 75% retention and exceeds a learned global selector by 4.70 points at 25%. On a fixed 200-page Ovis workload at the same 50% visual-token budget, only 3 of its outputs hit the length limit, versus 30-34 for the evaluated RTPrune, DivPrune, and HiPrune adaptations, and it finishes the batch 35-40% sooner. Code will be made publicly available.
authors: Yixuan Huang, ShengFan Zhang, Jiawei Chen
bullets: Targets a key OCR limitation: visually subtle symbols and repeated entries may be essential despite low salience.
Selects anchor tokens using adaptive resolution, global importance, and local contrast.
Compensates retained anchors with nearby discarded content and relative positions without adding tokens; the OCR backbone remains frozen.
At 50% of the original tokens, Ovis reaches 95.42 OmniDocBench Overall versus 96.09 uncompressed, and paired evaluations outperform simple input-resolution reduction.
At 25% retention, it exceeds a learned global selector by 4.70 points; at a 50% budget, it also reduces length-limit hits and finishes a fixed workload 35–40% sooner.

papers.selection_reason: Proposes a token compression framework for document OCR that preserves structural information while reducing visual token count, fitting the 'Token Pruning and Eviction' subtopic.
papers.title: Carry the Fine Print: Budget-Aware Visual Token Compression for Document OCR
papers.tldr: Select and Compensate compresses document OCR visual tokens by retaining informative anchors and enriching them with discarded local context, preserving near-full transcription quality at lower budgets.

papers.abstract: KV cache compression is critical for large reasoning models, where most of the cost comes from long generated reasoning traces rather than the input prompt. These traces often contain redundant and low-utility tokens due to looping, self-verification, and corrections. However, such tokens may still receive high attention scores, making it difficult to remove them without harming the reasoning process. We propose RoCoKV, a KV cache compression method designed for large reasoning models. RoCoKV introduces two key components. First, uncertainty-guided adaptive pruning adjusts the compression strength based on the model's confidence, allocating more memory during uncertain phases and applying stronger pruning when the model is confident. Second, redundancy-aware token selection reduces the impact of tokens that are highly similar to recent reasoning content, encouraging the model to retain more informative and diverse tokens. Beyond the algorithm, we co-design RoCoKV with the serving stack: we develop fused three-phase CUDA decode kernels and integrate them into vLLM as a drop-in plugin that preserves its paged KV layout and CUDA graph capture, turning algorithmic savings into real end-to-end speedups. Extensive experiments across three reasoning benchmarks and two reasoning models demonstrate that RoCoKV consistently improves reasoning accuracy under constrained KV cache budgets, achieving higher accuracy compared to state-of-the-art KV cache compression methods. For DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Llama-8B in vLLM, RoCoKV achieves a 1.27X speedup and 38% higher throughput on AIME25, the most challenging evaluated reasoning benchmark, and a 1.43X speedup and 45% higher throughput on the long synthetic benchmark, compared with Full-KV.
authors: Payman Behnam, Elaheh Sobhani, Saad Amin, Yahya Hassan, Daniyal Khan, Biswadeep Chakraborty, Tanish Patwa, Souvik Kundu, Alexey Tumanov
bullets: Targets redundant, low-utility tokens in long reasoning traces, which can nevertheless receive high attention scores.
Uses uncertainty-guided pruning: retains more cache during uncertain phases and prunes more aggressively when confidence is high.
Uses redundancy-aware selection to favor informative and diverse tokens over content similar to recent reasoning.
Co-designs the method with vLLM through fused CUDA decode kernels while preserving paged KV layout and CUDA graph capture.
Across three benchmarks and two reasoning models, improves accuracy under constrained cache budgets; for one 8B model, reports up to 1.43× speedup and 45% higher throughput versus Full-KV.

papers.abstract: Medical vision--language models (VLMs) often need to identify small, subtle lesions within high-resolution images containing extensive normal anatomy and redundant visual information. Visual-token compression improves efficiency, but preserving salient regions alone can discard the context needed for diagnostic interpretation. This context can extend across images: in bilateral mammography, the opposite breast provides a patient-specific anatomical reference. Yet retaining such evidence does not ensure that the model uses it effectively. We propose Bilateral Evidence Selection and Reasoning (BESR), which connects evidence preservation with comparative assessment through a bilateral-guided token selector and a bilateral reward. Under a shared token budget, the selector jointly prioritizes lesion appearance and its local and bilateral context, while the reward encourages assessments that benefit from the preserved comparison. Experiments on a bilateral dataset constructed from CBIS-DDSM and on VinDr-Mammo demonstrate improved evidence retention and diagnostic performance under constrained visual-token budgets. Inference benchmarking further shows reduced prefill latency.
authors: Zhengbo Zhou, Dooman Arefan, Shandong Wu
bullets: Addresses the risk that visual-token compression removes contextual information needed to interpret subtle mammographic lesions.
Uses a bilateral-guided token selector to prioritize lesions and their local and contralateral-breast context within a shared token budget.
Applies a bilateral reward to encourage diagnostic reasoning that benefits from preserved cross-image evidence.
Experiments on datasets built from CBIS-DDSM and VinDr-Mammo report better evidence retention and diagnostic performance under constrained token budgets.
Inference benchmarking shows reduced prefill latency.

papers.abstract: Memory consumption of the key-value (KV) cache remains a central bottleneck for long-context LLM inference. We introduce PRKV, a training-free KV eviction method that estimates multi-hop global token importance by applying Personalized PageRank over attention-induced transition graphs. This enables importance propagation beyond recency or instantaneous attention, without modifying the model. We benchmark PRKV on long-context understanding, sparse retrieval, and chain-of-thought reasoning tasks using multiple LLM families. Under moderate to aggressive compression ratios, including up to 90%, PRKV achieves competitive task performance against established eviction baselines while reducing peak memory usage with low end-to-end overhead. These results demonstrate that multi-hop global influence estimation yields a favorable accuracy--memory trade-off for scalable long-context inference.
authors: Seojin Kim, Noseong Park
bullets: Targets KV-cache memory bottlenecks in long-context LLM inference.
Propagates token importance across attention-induced transition graphs beyond recency or immediate attention.
Evaluated on long-context understanding, sparse retrieval, and chain-of-thought reasoning across multiple LLM families.
Maintains competitive task performance under moderate to aggressive compression, including up to 90%, with low end-to-end overhead.
Scope: performance is demonstrated across the reported tasks and model families, with a favorable accuracy–memory trade-off rather than universal superiority.

papers.selection_reason: Proposes a training-free KV cache eviction method based on global importance estimation, directly targeting memory-efficient LLM inference.
papers.title: Global Importance Estimation for KV Cache Eviction

papers.abstract: Self-attention over long token sequences dominates the inference cost of video diffusion transformers. Clustering-based sparse attention clusters both queries and keys and lets all queries in a cluster share one selection of key clusters. We show that this sharing limits accuracy: with key clusters and density fixed, attention grows more accurate as the query clusters are refined, and is most accurate when each query selects on its own, which needs no query clustering at all. We therefore propose Per-Query Routed Sparse Attention (PQRS), a training-free method that clusters only keys, lets each query select its own key clusters, and compensates for the unselected ones with their centroids. Per-query selections leave no query tile with a shared key list, so PQRS traverses key clusters instead of queries, buckets queries with identical selections into dense tasks, and merges their partial results in one pass under a fixed softmax offset carried from the previous denoising step. On four text-to-video and image-to-video models from the Wan and HunyuanVideo families, PQRS is the fastest of all the sparse attention methods we evaluate and the closest to the dense output, reaching $28.9$ dB PSNR on Wan2.1-T2V and $35.4$ dB on HunyuanVideo at $1.66$--$2.10\times$ end-to-end speedup.
authors: Zhen Huang, Shuwei Li, Ruizhe Yao, Xinrui Chen, Danyi Liu, Haoyuan Liang, Zhiyu Ye, Qiuyan Sun, Bingwei Chen, Yiyuan Li, Xu Zhou, Haohuan Fu
bullets: Clustering queries and keys together limits sparse-attention accuracy because queries in a cluster share key selections.
PQRS clusters only keys, performs per-query key-cluster selection, and approximates unselected keys with cluster centroids.
It efficiently executes per-query routing by grouping queries with identical selections and merging results with a carried softmax offset.
Evaluated on four Wan and HunyuanVideo text-to-video and image-to-video models, it achieves 1.66–2.10× end-to-end speedup.
It reports 28.9 dB PSNR on Wan2.1-T2V and 35.4 dB on HunyuanVideo, while remaining closest to dense attention among evaluated sparse methods.

papers.abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) can answer questions about long interleaved inputs, such as documents of many pages and collections of hundreds of images, but they are slow to start: on inputs of about 100K tokens, the prefill takes most of the wait for the first output token. A common approach prunes the input by scoring its tokens with the target model itself or with a small model of the same family that first writes an answer. However, this scoring takes much of the time that pruning saves. We find that the evidence for a question lies in a few whole units (images or paragraphs), and that a small hybrid model finds them with one attention head of an early layer, even at half image resolution. Based on these findings, we propose SkimPrefill, which lets the small hybrid model read the whole input first, up to that early layer, with images at half resolution. Most layers of the small hybrid model (Qwen3.5-0.8B) run in linear time, so this pass is short. SkimPrefill then ranks every unit with that head and gives the target the top units as an ordinary shorter prompt. One untrained selector serves targets of different model families. Extensive experiments on MMLongBench at 128K tokens, with 19 datasets of five task types, show the effectiveness of SkimPrefill. With 10% of the input tokens kept, SkimPrefill speeds up the prefill of Qwen3.5-9B, Gemma-4-12B and Qwen3-VL-32B by 3.7 times, 11.6 time and 8.2 times while maintaining their average accuracy.
authors: Xiaolin Lin, Kai-Chiang Wu, Bing Li, Grace Li Zhang
bullets: Targets the high first-token latency caused by prefill on roughly 100K-token interleaved image-text inputs.
Uses an early attention head in a small hybrid model, with images at half resolution, to rank whole input units.
Keeps the top 10% of tokens/units and feeds them to the target VLM as a shorter ordinary prompt.
A single untrained selector transfers across different target model families.
On MMLongBench at 128K tokens, it maintains average accuracy while reporting 3.7×, 11.6×, and 8.2× prefill speedups for three target models.

papers.title: Let a Small Model Read First: Faster Prefill for Long Interleaved Image-Text Inputs
papers.tldr: SkimPrefill accelerates long-context VLMs by using a small model to identify relevant images and paragraphs before the target model processes a shortened prompt.

papers.abstract: LLM-based agents accumulate extensive interaction histories when solving complex, long-horizon tasks, making efficient memory management critical to their performance and scalability. While existing memory management methods primarily focus on what to retain or retrieve, they often overlook how much perceptual detail should be allocated to individual past interactions. We posit that effective agent memory depends not only on the information preserved, but also on the granularity at which each past interaction is perceived. Motivated by this insight, we propose Resolution as Attention (RAA), a memory perception mechanism that uses visual resolution as a means of attention allocation across interaction histories. RAA renders past interactions as images and dynamically adjusts their resolution at every step according to their relevance to the agent's upcoming decision, preserving fine-grained information for critical interactions while reducing visual-token consumption for less relevant ones. To adaptively determine the perceptual fidelity of each interaction, we train a lightweight relevance estimator with teacher-model guidance and further optimize it to preserve the agent's decision consistency at a reduced visual-token cost. Experiments across multiple tasks and backbones show that RAA reduces token consumption by over 50% without compromising task performance. Moreover, RAA can be integrated as a plug-in perception layer with existing memory management methods, yielding further token savings and revealing adaptive perception as a complementary dimension of agent memory.
authors: Siqi Xiang, Zhipeng Xu, Shengrui Liu, Zulong Chen, Chunyan Miao, Shijian Lu
bullets: Targets inefficient perception of long interaction histories in LLM-based agents.
Renders past interactions as images and allocates resolution according to relevance to the next decision.
Uses a lightweight, teacher-guided relevance estimator optimized to preserve decision consistency.
Works across multiple tasks and backbones and can complement existing memory management methods.
Scope: focuses on adaptive perceptual granularity rather than deciding what memories to retain or retrieve.

papers.selection_reason: Introduces a memory perception mechanism that dynamically adjusts the resolution of past interactions to reduce token consumption, directly addressing token efficiency and agent memory.
papers.title: Resolution as Attention for Efficient Agent Memory Perception

papers.abstract: AI agents read their whole history at every step. People do not work like that: we keep what the moment needs and hold the rest as a rough note we can recall. MoE-Context applies this to language models. The context is split into blocks. Before each step a fast yes or no pass decides which blocks the step needs; the rest stay as one-line notes that can be brought back, and nothing is deleted. In the version we build, one model makes this decision and then answers, over a single key-value cache where hidden blocks are masked rather than removed. On a laptop with Qwen3-1.7B and a synthetic lookup task, showing only the needed block raises accuracy from 93 to 119 of 120, and a masked block is as hidden as a deleted one. The model's own picking is the weak part. A supervised linear probe written into spare output rows lifts its accuracy from 80 to 110 of 120, but simple keyword search picks perfectly on this task, and the probe does not transfer to a second task. We report these results openly, along with two cheap usage patterns that block switching enables: undoing a failed attempt and running subagents without a new context.
authors: Vedant Navale
bullets: Splits history into blocks and uses a fast yes/no selector to reveal relevant blocks while masking others in one key-value cache.
On a synthetic lookup task with Qwen3-1.7B, selective context improved accuracy from 93/120 to 119/120; masking was comparable to deletion.
Context selection is the main weakness: a supervised linear probe reached 110/120, while keyword search achieved perfect task performance.
The probe did not transfer to a second task, limiting evidence for general-purpose selection.
Block switching also supports undoing failed attempts and running subagents without creating a new context.

papers.tldr: MoE-Context lets language models selectively expose only the context blocks needed for each step while preserving the rest as recoverable notes.

papers.abstract: Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs) are expected to achieve semantic reasoning, intelligent decision-making, and long-horizon navigation under strict onboard constraints. While recent foundation-model-driven approaches have shown promising progress toward this goal, existing methods remain limited by challenges in 3D data availability, trajectory feasibility, long-horizon reasoning, and computational efficiency in complex environments. To bridge these gaps, we propose VLN-AR, a hierarchical vision-language-navigation (VLN) framework for aerial robots. VLN-AR decouples multimodal reasoning and low-level control, enabling structured prediction of 3D pose commands and navigation intentions that are translated into dynamically feasible actions. To mitigate data scarcity and domain gaps, we introduce a fully automated 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS)-based pipeline to generate scalable photorealistic UAV navigation data. A progressive three-stage training strategy further enhances grounding, scene reasoning, and complex navigation. In addition, a lightweight cognitive agent improves long-horizon reasoning via memory-aware task decomposition. Finally, we design onboard optimization techniques, including token sparsification and model lightweighting, achieving 7.1x-9.4x speedup while maintaining high navigation performance on resource-limited UAV platforms. Experiments show great improvements over existing methods in both simulation and real-world UAV navigation. Project website: https://wyz000.github.io/VLN-AR/
authors: Yuze Wu, Mo Zhu, Xingxing Li, Yuheng Du, Zhaoqi Wang, Yuxin Fan, Wenjun Li, Kenghou Hoi, Zhichao Han, Xin Zhou, Fei Gao
bullets: Separates multimodal reasoning from low-level control by predicting 3D poses and navigation intentions that are converted into dynamically feasible actions.
Uses an automated 3D Gaussian Splatting pipeline to generate scalable, photorealistic UAV navigation data and address data scarcity and domain gaps.
Employs progressive three-stage training for improved grounding, scene reasoning, and complex navigation.
Adds a memory-aware cognitive agent for long-horizon task decomposition and onboard optimizations such as token sparsification and model lightweighting.
Reports 7.1×–9.4× speedups while maintaining high navigation performance, with improvements demonstrated in simulation and real-world UAV experiments.

papers.abstract: Long video understanding remains a daunting challenge for existing multimodal large language models (MLLMs), mainly due to the large number of visual tokens accumulated in long videos. Currently, frame selection and token selection are two main paradigms for addressing this issue, both aiming to select relevant visual information to form a compact input for MLLMs. A natural approach combines these two paradigms by selecting frames before pruning tokens, but noisy frame-level relevance estimates can cause irreversible evidence loss. In this paper, we study this problem from the perspective of assessing the spatiotemporal distribution of query-specific evidence and propose a novel and training-free approach termed NULLTOK. For every patch across all frames, we construct an empirical-null distribution from 64 group-matched irrelevant control queries, capturing the scores expected in the absence of target-specific evidence. Target affinities are calibrated against these same-position references into right-tail Monte Carlo p-values, which are discrete super-uniform under a conditional exchangeability assumption. Calibrated screening and a high-recall semantic guard produce candidate tokens for deterministic visual deduplication and joint spatiotemporal budget allocation. To validate NullTok, we apply it to two representative MLLMs and conduct extensive experiments on a set of video benchmarks. The experimental results demonstrate its effectiveness under a bounded visual token budget. For example, it achieves 65.81% and 68.85% on Video-MME using frozen LLaVA-Video-7B and Qwen3-VL-8B backbones, respectively, at a cap of 64 full-frame equivalents (FFE), without subtitles or audio. These results outperform all evaluated baselines on Video-MME under the same budget for both backbones. Code is available at https://github.com/potato-kitty/NullTok.
authors: Zhang Ziyue, Juwei Jian, Baiyang Song, Yunshan Zhong, Jun Peng, Yiyi Zhou, Rongrong Ji
bullets: Addresses evidence loss caused by selecting frames before pruning tokens in long videos.
Builds position-matched empirical-null distributions from irrelevant control queries and converts affinities into Monte Carlo p-values.
Combines calibrated screening with a high-recall semantic guard, deduplication, and joint spatiotemporal budget allocation.
Evaluated with frozen LLaVA-Video-7B and Qwen3-VL-8B on video benchmarks without subtitles or audio.
On Video-MME at 64 full-frame equivalents, achieves 65.81% and 68.85%, outperforming evaluated baselines for the respective backbones.

papers.tldr: NullTok is a training-free method that selects query-relevant video tokens using empirical-null calibration, enabling long-video understanding within a fixed visual-token budget.

papers.abstract: Reasoning vision-language models (VLMs) think for thousands of tokens before they answer, and retention policies keep the KV cache affordable by pruning it as the reasoning grows. We find that this pruning sacrifices the image in multi-turn conversations: the image and the reasoning share one budget, so the growing reasoning crowds the visual entries out. A chart question that loses 8 points to the full cache when asked first loses 24 points when asked after a round of reasoning. Protecting a small visual reserve from eviction recovers most of this loss, while adding the same slots to the shared budget recovers considerably less. The image therefore lacks protection, not capacity. Based on this finding, we propose ShelfKV, a training-free method that works on top of existing retention policies. It keeps every visual entry in CPU memory and, at each decoding step, swaps the visual entries that the current query scores highest into the attention slots of the text entries it scores lowest. The image is never evicted, yet it occupies attention slots only while it is read. We evaluate ShelfKV on four benchmarks, three of them conversational, with two retention policies and two reasoning VLMs. In conversations, it improves the strongest existing policy, DBTrimKV, by up to 20.3 points at matched GPU memory, and still leads by 8.7 points when DBTrimKV uses twice the memory. It also consistently outperforms a fixed visual reserve of matched GPU memory in these settings, without hurting accuracy on standalone questions. These results show that the image should be protected from the reasoning but read only on demand.
authors: Ziyi Wang, Xiyue Zhang, Bing Hu, Guangmin Song, Chenyi Zhang, Li Wang
bullets: Problem: KV-cache pruning lets growing reasoning tokens evict image tokens, causing larger accuracy losses in later conversational turns.
Method: Keep all visual entries in CPU memory and dynamically swap query-relevant visual entries into slots occupied by low-scoring text entries.
Training-free and compatible with existing retention policies, including DBTrimKV.
Across four benchmarks, two retention policies, and two reasoning VLMs, ShelfKV improves DBTrimKV by up to 20.3 points at matched GPU memory and 8.7 points when DBTrimKV has twice the memory.
It outperforms a fixed visual reserve in conversational settings without reducing standalone-question accuracy.

papers.title: Keep the Reasoning, Read the Image: On-Demand Visual KV for Multi-Turn Reasoning VLMs
papers.tldr: ShelfKV preserves visual information during long multi-turn VLM reasoning by swapping relevant image tokens into attention slots on demand, substantially improving accuracy without extra GPU memory.

papers.abstract: Spiking Neural Networks (SNNs) promise event-driven and energy-efficient vision, yet existing spiking vision transformers (S-ViTs) largely confine spiking tokens to fixed and uniform firing schemes along the temporal, spatial and channel dimensions, whereas suppressing the computational redundancy thus incurred calls for adaptive firing mechanisms that operate jointly across all three axes at test time. To this end, we propose the Adaptive Efficient Integrate-and-Fire (AdaE-IF) model, which consults the attention score of each spiking token and routes salient regions to fine-grained firing patterns while assigning energy-frugal coarse patterns to the remaining regions. Building on AdaE-IF, we further introduce Spiking Gated Self-Attention (S-GSA) and Spiking Local-Gated Unit (S-LGU), which enforce selective spike emission at token and channel granularity. We integrate the aforementioned mechanisms and modules into AdaS-ViT, a test-time adaptive-routing architecture trained with a progressive spatio-temporal curriculum that stabilizes the co-adaptation of firing precision and routing masks. Extensive experiments across benchmarks spanning diverse data scales and modalities demonstrate that AdaS-ViT consistently achieves highly competitive performance. Notably, on ImageNet-1k it consumes only 1.02 to 2.45 millijoules per image and attains an accuracy-per-energy ratio of 32$\times$ to 72$\times$, operating in an economical inference regime and thereby pushing the energy-efficiency boundary further.
authors: Zecheng Hao, Zihan Huang, Shenghao Xie, Jiyuan Zhang, Zhaofei Yu, Tiejun Huang
bullets: Addresses redundant computation from fixed, uniform firing patterns in spiking vision transformers.
Uses attention-guided AdaE-IF routing to assign fine-grained firing to salient regions and coarse firing elsewhere.
Adds S-GSA and S-LGU for selective spike emission at token and channel granularity.
Trains routing and firing precision with a progressive spatio-temporal curriculum.
On ImageNet-1k, reports 1.02–2.45 mJ per image and a 32×–72× accuracy-per-energy ratio.

figures.caption: Figure 3. Architecture of AdaS-ViT. Top: the macro pipeline stacks dual-mode AdaS-Blocks (S-GSA followed by S-LGU or S-FFN) over progressively downsampled token maps. Bottom: data flow of S-GSA, S-LGU and the parameterized S-FFN variants (I)(II) with convolution kernel size k and expansion ratio r.

Figure 4. Fine-grained energy breakdown of AdaS-ViT Large on ImageNet-1k. Module-level (a)–(c) and Operator-level (d)–(f) statistics of SOPs and average spike firing rates. For each block, Bar hues identify the module family, the total height of a bar denotes the theoretical SOPs Upper-bound while its dark lower segment denotes the actually incurred SOPs, the curve on the right axis reports the average firing rate.

Figure 1. AdaS-ViT establishes a compelling accuracy-energy frontier for spiking vision transformers. (a) Qualitative comparison of training paradigms over six axes covering training cost and inference behavior: prior paradigms trade these objectives against one another, whereas our test-time adaptive routing maintains a uniformly strong profile across all of them. (b) Quantitative comparison with prior SNN-based works on ImageNet-1k. The horizontal axis denotes top-1 accuracy and the vertical axis reports Ratio AE, i.e., the accuracy delivered per millijoule of inference energy. AdaS-ViT occupies the top-right region alone with the smallest bubble area, indicating markedly higher energy efficiency at a fraction of the parameters of prior art.

Figure 2. AdaE-IF: from uniform to adaptive and efficient spike firing. Top-left: the firing-rate curve of a vanilla IF/LIF neuron is ideally a uniform staircase, yet diverse input current patterns {Ilt} yield divergent firing rates F̃l 1:T for identical average input current Ĩl1:T , which accumulate across layers into conversion error and spatio-temporal gradient inconsistency. Bottom: AdaE-IF maps each spike firing pattern to its bit-granular equivalent, aligning training gradients and enabling precise regulation of Synaptic Operations (SOPs); guided by the attention score of the spiking feature map (Middle), it routes each token to a coarse-grained pattern that preserves energy efficiency, or a fine-grained pattern that enhances representation at only marginal extra cost; jointly scheduled under an ultra-low energy budget (Top-right), the two modes realize test-time adaptive firing precision.

papers.selection_reason: Test-time adaptive token routing in spiking vision transformers to suppress computational redundancy, fitting efficient AI and test-time adaptation.
papers.title: AdaS-ViT: Test-Time Adaptive Routing for Spiking Vision Transformers with Ultra-High Energy Efficiency
papers.tldr: AdaS-ViT adaptively routes spiking tokens across temporal, spatial, and channel dimensions to maintain competitive vision performance with very low inference energy.

papers.abstract: Audio-visual question answering on lightweight user devices requires balancing speed, memory usage, privacy, and communication. One approach is to run audio-visual encoders on a server and a lightweight language decoder on the user device, keeping questions local while offloading media encoding. However, transferring and processing the full multimodal representation remains costly. We propose a training-free, query-agnostic token pruning framework that constructs a compact, reusable memory before transmission. We define video spatio-temporal blocks and aligned audio windows as players and estimate their importance through Monte Carlo Shapley valuation. We use an embedding coverage objective that combines query-independent utility with cross-modal redundancy calibration and rewards unimodal diversity through marginal coverage gains. We retain the original token embeddings of high-scoring players under a limited token budget and transfer the resulting memory once for reuse across subsequent local questions. Experiments on Video-MME, Daily-Omni, and Video-Holmes using video-SALMONN 2+ (3B) and video-SALMONN 2 Pro (4B) show that our method achieves the best or tied-best QA accuracy among the compared compression methods across all evaluated settings. On Daily-Omni with video-SALMONN 2+ (3B) at 80\% pruning, our method improves accuracy by 12.86--14.62 percentage points over these methods while achieving the lowest device-side LLM prefill and decoding latency, with up to $1.92\times$ decoding speedup at comparable embedding memory usage.
authors: Qitong Wang, Jihui Jin, Divya Kothandaraman, Vishnu Raj, Christopher Rasmussen
bullets: Targets the cost of transferring and processing full multimodal representations on lightweight devices.
Estimates the importance of spatio-temporal video blocks and aligned audio windows using Monte Carlo Shapley valuation.
Uses query-agnostic embedding coverage to balance utility, cross-modal redundancy, and unimodal diversity under a token budget.
Retains original embeddings for reuse across multiple local questions, avoiding repeated media transmission.
Across three benchmarks and two models, it matches or exceeds competing compression methods; in one setting, it improves accuracy by 12.86–14.62 points and reaches up to 1.92× decoding speedup.

figures.caption: Figure 1. A server processes video and audio into a compact memory and transfers it once to a personal device. The device reuses this memory to answer multiple questions locally, keeping user queries on the device. To construct the compact memory, we propose a novel token selection method. Fig. 2 provides an overview of our framework and the proposed method.

Figure 2. (a) The server encodes audio-visual content, constructs token groups as players, and performs query-agnostic selection to build a compact multimodal memory. The memory is transferred once to a lightweight device and reused to answer subsequent questions locally. Selection considers unimodal utility, intra-modal diversity, and cross-modal redundancy. (b) Video players are formed from spatio-temporal token blocks, while audio players group tokens aligned with the corresponding temporal intervals. Colors illustrate example groups in each modality. (c) We estimate each player’s Shapley value by Monte Carlo sampling of player permutations using a weighted coverage function that captures intra-modal diversity through cosine similarity of embeddings (i.e., e). The weights incorporate unimodal utility, derived from token-embedding L2 norms as a proxy for semantic informativeness, and cross-modal redundancy, measured by cosine similarity between players from different modalities. Players with higher estimated Shapley values are retained, while lower-scoring players are pruned.

Figure 3. Each row shows the same sampled frames for a different method, with retained regions highlighted and pruned regions darkened. Our method better preserves key objects and complementary action-related cues across the displayed frames, including the skateboard, foot placement, and the demonstrator’s body. “Q” and “A” denote the question about the video content and its corresponding ground-truth answer, respectively.

Figure 4. Network-aware amortized latency under different assumed bandwidths (25, 50, 100, and 300 Mbps). Server-side encoding and pruning are excluded under the assumption that queryagnostic memory is precomputed and cached before online question answering. Transfer latency is analytically estimated from the memory payload size, while LLM inference costs are obtained from measured stage-wise timings. Lower is better.

Table 1. QA accuracy (%) on three benchmarks using two backbones. The pruning ratio denotes the percentage of removed multimodal tokens. Full Tokens denotes the unpruned model. The best results are marked in bold.

Table 2. Ablation studies using video-SALMONN 2+ (3B) at a 90% pruning ratio. We investigate the number of Monte Carlo samples and the contributions of different value function components. The best results are highlighted in bold.

Table 3. We report the average LLM prefill and decoding latency, together with the memory of retained input embeddings, assuming a hidden dimension of 2048 and BF16 precision. The best results are highlighted in bold.

papers.selection_reason: Training-free token pruning and eviction for compact audio-visual memory; directly fits efficient AI.
papers.title: Transfer Once, Ask Locally: Compact Audio-Visual Memory for On-Device Question Answering
papers.tldr: A training-free method prunes audio-visual tokens into a compact memory that is transferred once and reused for fast, private on-device question answering.

papers.abstract: Looped vision-language models (VLMs) deepen computation by reusing shared layers, approaching larger models' capabilities with fewer parameters and easing the storage and deployment burden of stacking independent layers. However, repeatedly processing long visual sequences still incurs substantial compute and GPU memory costs. Visual token compression reduces these costs by shortening sequences. Existing methods mainly select original tokens directly or combine selection with aggregation. In looped models, the former may overlook changing token importance across calls and discard information needed later; the latter lack joint consideration of output changes across calls, limiting information preservation. We propose LoopZip, a training-free visual token compression algorithm addressing both issues. Visual aggregation builds a compact candidate pool before the looped backbone, and cross-invocation selection averages instruction attention from the first two existing calls of the same shared attention layer to retain tokens needed by both states. Weight-tied value correction then jointly fits shared visual-value adjustments to both pre-selection layer outputs, reducing output deviations across states. To validate LoopZip's effectiveness, we conduct extensive experiments covering two open-source looped VLMs, eleven benchmarks, and three pruning ratios. On LoopVL-1B, LoopZip retains 97.16% of the original model's performance at 50% pruning ratio and exceeds the strongest baseline by 5.36% at 87.5% pruning ratio. Across Hugging Face Transformers, vLLM, and SGLang, LoopVL-1B with LoopZip reduces peak allocated GPU memory by 58.36%-58.98% and achieves 2.01-2.47x end-to-end speedups over the original model.
authors: Weizhong Huang, Zhicheng Liu, Yan Zhang, Fei Chao, Xiawu Zheng, Liujuan Cao
bullets: Targets the high compute and GPU-memory cost of repeatedly processing long visual-token sequences in looped VLMs.
Builds a compact candidate pool through visual aggregation before the looped backbone.
Selects tokens using averaged instruction attention from the first two calls of shared layers, capturing changing token importance across states.
Applies weight-tied value correction to reduce output deviations after pruning.

Across two looped VLMs and eleven benchmarks, it retains 97.16% performance at 50% pruning and delivers up to 58.98% lower peak GPU memory and 2.47× speedup; scope is limited to the evaluated models, benchmarks, and pruning ratios.
papers.selection_reason: Visual token compression for looped vision-language models; combines token pruning with cross-invocation selection and reduces memory/compute in VLMs.
papers.title: LoopZip: Visual Token Compression for Efficient Looped Vision-Language Models
papers.tldr: LoopZip is a training-free visual-token compression method for looped VLMs that preserves performance while substantially reducing memory use and inference time.

papers.abstract: Reference-to-video diffusion transformers pack the variational autoencoder (VAE) latents of all references and the generated tokens into one full-attention sequence, in which reference tokens make up about half. Because attention cost grows quadratically with sequence length, these tokens take up an even larger share of the attention computation, yet most of them are static, smooth or irrelevant to the output. To accelerate reference-conditioned generation, we propose pruning and caching of reference tokens for video generation (PCRG), a training-free, plug-and-play method that uses two signals the model already computes to assign each reference token to one of three tiers, namely pruned, cached or kept. The first is a low-level redundancy r from VAE latents, since a token whose latent barely changes over time or across its neighbors adds little new content. The second is a high-level importance g from the vision-language-model (VLM) conditioner, where the attention that the prompt and any first or last frames pay to a token tells whether the output needs to read it. Tokens that are not redundant are kept, and redundant tokens are cached if important and pruned otherwise. Pruned tokens leave the sequence before the first step with all rotary position embedding positions unchanged. Cached tokens have their keys and values computed once and reused, and kept tokens are processed as usual. On MiniMax-H3, already distilled to 8 timesteps and quantized to int8, PCRG is 1.57x faster end to end on our V2V-Bench and 1.49x faster on the public VACE-Benchmark, while the quality of VBench drops by only 0.24% and 0.17%, respectively. PCRG shortens the sequence rather than changing how attention is computed or which steps are run, so it also stacks on step caching and sparse attention. On V2V-Bench it reaches 1.86x with TeaCache, 1.82x with Spark at nearly unchanged fidelity and 2.15x with Veda.
authors: Siyuan Wang, Haoran Li, Yi Yue, Tak L. Fung, Quan Chen
bullets: Targets the quadratic attention cost caused by reference tokens, which comprise roughly half of the sequence.
Ranks tokens using latent redundancy and VLM-derived importance, assigning them to prune, cache, or keep tiers.
Pruned tokens are removed before generation while preserving rotary positions; cached tokens reuse their keys and values.
Achieves 1.57× and 1.49× end-to-end speedups on two benchmarks with only 0.24% and 0.17% VBench quality drops.
Combines with existing acceleration methods, reaching up to 2.15× speedup in the reported experiments.

papers.selection_reason: Training-free pruning and caching of reference tokens in video diffusion transformers; directly targets token-level efficiency and video generation acceleration.
papers.title: PCRG: Training-Free Pruning and Caching of Reference Tokens for Video Generation
papers.tldr: PCRG accelerates reference-conditioned video generation by training-free pruning and caching of redundant reference tokens with minimal quality loss.

papers.abstract: JEPA-style latent world models let embodied agents plan toward new goals with model predictive control, but they are still too slow for real-life embodied control: sampling-based MPC repeats predictor inference tens of thousands of times per plan, and even on high-end GPUs one planning step can take tens of seconds. We observe substantial latent locality in this repeated-inference workload: the predictor maps close actions to close latents, and inside a quantized predictor this closeness takes a form that hardware can exploit, differential bit-level sparsity. Unlike an input stream, whose temporal similarity is given, a planner itself decides which candidates it evaluates together, so the planner can choose its own references and, with reference forest sampling, manufacture more sparsity: it couples the sampled action sequences of each group to a shared root, with competitive planning quality. We build the accelerator on the insights of the rich line of bit-level sparsity accelerators and design it and the planner tightly coupled as a single co-design: the planner increases sparsity and exposes structure for hardware scheduling, and the bit-exact hardware effectively uses the sparsity that the planner creates. On three JEPA world models, our co-design is 1.28-1.80x faster than a dense accelerator and uses 38-52% less energy, and it is 1.22-1.58x faster than prior bit-sparse design and uses 16-36% less energy, with the same area. To our knowledge, our planner is the first planner that manufactures differential bit-level sparsity across its candidates and exposes its structure for hardware scheduling, and our co-design is the first algorithm-hardware co-design for JEPA-style world-model planning.
authors: Wenbo Zhu, Paul Yi-Chia Chen, Yuanhan Li, Zishen Wan, Christopher Torng
bullets: JEPA world-model planning is slow because sampling-based MPC repeatedly runs predictor inference at large scale.
The method groups action sequences around shared reference roots, manufacturing latent similarity and hardware-exploitable differential sparsity.
A tightly coupled accelerator uses this sparsity and planner-exposed structure for efficient scheduling.
Across three JEPA world models, it achieves 1.28–1.80× speedup and 38–52% lower energy than a dense accelerator.
Compared with prior bit-sparse hardware at the same area, it achieves 1.22–1.58× speedup and 16–36% lower energy.

papers.selection_reason: Directly addresses efficient planning with JEPA-style latent world models by introducing differential bit-level sparsity. This combines World Models (Latent Action Models) with Efficient AI (Token Pruning) through a planner-hardware co-design.
papers.title: Manufacturing Differential Sparsity: Planner-Hardware Co-Design for Efficient World Model Planning
papers.tldr: A planner–hardware co-design accelerates JEPA-style world-model MPC by deliberately creating differential bit-level sparsity among candidate action sequences.

papers.abstract: Visual token pruning speeds up large vision-language models (VLMs) by keeping only a part of their visual tokens. Most existing methods improve the ranking of the tokens and then answer every question once with the same budget. With strong rankings, pruning hurts only a few questions, and signals computed on the kept tokens see little of what it removed. We find that, on most of these questions, a small VLM given the full image disagrees with the pruned answer, since it still sees the missing evidence. We propose PRUDENT, which first answers with about half the budget and spends the saved tokens on re-answering the disagreeing questions at twice the budget. We show when such re-answering pays and why the small VLM should read the full image. On 18 benchmarks, PRUDENT outperforms eight existing pruning methods at the same average budget of visual tokens. Its lead widens as the budget tightens, and holds across five InternVL sizes. PRUDENT also has the highest average in two more model families. The disagreement of the small VLM flags most pruning failures of all eight methods, and re-answering on it also improves the two strongest with their own rankings. Other checkers give similar gains, and the extra tokens go where the first pass hurts the answer. These results suggest that identifying which pruned answers are trustworthy provides an additional lever for visual token pruning beyond the ranking of tokens. Code and data are available at https://github.com/LiZaiyuan0619/PRUDENT.
authors: Yanchao Li, Jiaqing Xie, Ben Gao, Yusu Zhang, Beilun Wang, Yanbo Wang, Xiaohua Xu, Zhongyu Huang, Tianfan Fu, Nanqing Dong
bullets: Existing pruning methods typically use one fixed token budget for every question, even though pruning harms only some answers.
PRUDENT first answers with roughly half the token budget, then reallocates saved tokens to questions where a small full-image VLM disagrees with the pruned answer.
Across 18 benchmarks, it outperforms eight pruning methods at the same average visual-token budget, with larger gains under tighter budgets.
The disagreement signal identifies most pruning failures and also improves strong existing pruning methods and multiple VLM families.
The approach focuses extra computation on uncertain answers rather than improving token ranking alone.

papers.abstract: Occlusions and limited sensor range make ego-only 3D perception insufficient for safe driving. Collaborative perception addresses this by enabling connected vehicles to share complementary observations, yet it remains constrained by tight vehicular communication budgets. While spatial selection is more flexible than fixed-rate feature compression, existing selectors remain largely sender-driven and waste scarce bandwidth on ego-visible targets. Furthermore, applying convolutions after masking spreads isolated tokens into their neighborhoods, silently violating low-bandwidth constraints. To address this, we propose Spatial Elastic Consensus (SEC), a bandwidth-adaptive framework centered on bilateral demand-supply consensus. Instead of unilateral token selection, the ego vehicle formulates a content-aware demand prior while each collaborator evaluates its local supply. This single-round consensus allocates the token budget to critical ego-missed evidence rather than ego-visible redundancy, without transmitting dense maps. To guarantee exact budget compliance, an anti-dilation refine-before-mask pipeline refines features prior to discrete token selection, preventing receptive-field leakage. A lightweight deformable sampler then aggregates these sparse messages with learned local offsets, compensating for the spatial context lost to token selection and mitigating inter-agent pose drift. Evaluated at a stringent 64KiB budget, SEC consistently achieves the best AP@0.7 on the simulated OPV2V and V2XSet datasets and the real-world DAIR-V2X dataset. These results demonstrate that combining bilateral consensus with budget-exact transmission is key to efficient low-bandwidth collaborative perception.
authors: Linshan Yan
bullets: Addresses occlusions and limited sensor range that make ego-only perception unsafe.
Uses bilateral demand–supply consensus: the ego proposes content-aware needs, while collaborators assess available evidence.
Refines features before discrete masking to prevent convolutional receptive-field leakage and guarantee budget-exact transmission.
Applies lightweight deformable sampling to recover local context and reduce effects of token sparsity and pose drift.
At 64KiB, achieves the best AP@0.7 across simulated OPV2V/V2XSet and real-world DAIR-V2X evaluations.

papers.abstract: Generative retrieval (GR) predicts catalog entries as short semantic identifiers (SIDs). Trie-constrained beam search keeps these identifiers valid, but wide beams expose two serving costs: vocabulary-wide score tensors that are mostly discarded, and repeated attention over the same prompt. We present Trie-Head, a model-native output interface that stores the identifier trie as validated GPU tensors. Compared with a Python custom logit processor (CLP), it reduces CPU--GPU coordination and memory traffic by avoiding Python constraint callbacks and vocabulary-wide candidate buffers. It scores compact codebook candidates and streams the full-vocabulary normalizer, preserving the original model's valid-token scores in real arithmetic without retraining. Shared-context attention complements this output path by reusing prompt key/value blocks across beams while preserving their private decode tails. We implement both mechanisms in SGLang and evaluate candidate sourcing for LinkedIn Hiring Assistant and qualification retrieval for the Qualification Retrieval Platform. The combined system improves closed-loop throughput by up to 5.57x over the CLP baseline and up to 2.63x over BF16 FlashRec at a common beam width of 200 on the Qualification Retrieval Platform workload.
authors: Vedant Jhaveri, Arashpreet Singh Mor, Satyam Kumar, Alex Tsun, Qing Lan, Shaunak Mishra, Sriram Vasudevan

Scores compact codebook candidates while streaming the full-vocabulary normalizer to preserve the model’s valid-token scores.
Shared-context attention reuses prompt key/value blocks while keeping beam-specific decode tails.
Implemented in SGLang; the combined system achieves up to 5.57× throughput over CLP and 2.63× over BF16 FlashRec at beam width 200 on one workload.

papers.abstract: Block-wise diffusion language models (DLMs) refine multiple tokens in parallel, offering an alternative to token-by-token autoregressive decoding. Their long-context inference, however, remains bottlenecked by memory-bound attention: every denoising step repeatedly reads a growing historical key--value (KV) cache. Directly applying sparse attention does not fully solve this problem, because different queries can select different pages, inflating the block's collective read set, while repeated support construction adds overhead and permanent eviction can discard information needed later. We present RISA, a recoverable sparse-attention method with shared read plans for block-wise DLMs. RISA exploits the fact that historical KV remains fixed within a block while queries evolve across denoising steps. Newly generated history is organized into exact priority and recovery tiers; seed queries then build a protected, bounded read plan whose indices are reused across the block while attention is recomputed with fresh queries and current-block KV. This separates history preservation from repeated reading and amortizes sparse-support construction without changing the backbone or decoder. On DreamReasoner-8B, RISA retains comparable task performance. At 32K, the default configuration speeds up attention by $2.67\times$ and fixed-trajectory requests by $1.36\times$ over dense, and attention speedup reaches $5.53\times$ at 128K. Across eight settings on three models, RISA decodes faster than the tested MAGE, QUEST, and LoSA budgets at matched KL.
authors: Xinrui Zhong, Fanjiang Ye, Yuke Wang
bullets: Targets memory-bound attention caused by repeatedly reading growing historical KV caches.
Builds shared read plans from seed queries using exact priority and recovery tiers, while recomputing attention with fresh queries and current-block KV.
Protects potentially useful history from permanent eviction and amortizes sparse-support construction without modifying the backbone or decoder.
On DreamReasoner-8B, it preserves comparable task performance and reports up to 5.53× attention speedup at 128K context.
Across eight settings and three models, it decodes faster than tested MAGE, QUEST, and LoSA budgets at matched KL.

papers.abstract: Sparse attention models read a few blocks of keys for every query at a fixed budget and can lose much of their long-context retrieval accuracy at that budget. We ask where this loss is made. Using exact attention mass selection at the shipped budget as an oracle, we show that the selector under-ranks the needle rather than running out of budget. We find attention heads that miss the needle by running a calibration probe that teacher-forces the answer and reads two quantities in every head. The first is the needle attention that the selector forfeits, and the second is the share of the answer's log-probability that fixing the head's selection restores, integrated along the path from the shipped selector to full attention. Four checkpoints of the InfLLM-V2 family and NOSA-8B lose multi-key retrieval in the same three blind heads, which attend to the needle while a mean-pooled key summary dilutes its single decisive token. Full attention in those heads or a 4-bit scorer that keeps the shipped budget recovers most of the loss without training. On MiniCPM4.1-8B at 64K, either fix lifts multi-key retrieval accuracy from 54.1 to 97.5%, level with full attention in every head. In production serving engines, full attention in those heads keeps 84 to 89% of the time to first token (TTFT) that sparse attention saves at 32K to 128K context length. Beyond the InfLLM-V2 selector lineage, one unified rule flags attention heads above a threshold swept on each checkpoint until they close most of the gap to full attention on calibration prompts. A similar small set of blind attention heads carry the loss for the SeerAttention-R gates, NSA, and DashAttention, whereas many such heads exist in MoBA. On Qwen3-8B with the SeerAttention-R gates, full attention in 18 of 288 key-value heads lifts multi-key retrieval accuracy from 29.8 to 97.7%.
authors: Wenhe Zhang, Boxing Chen
bullets: Exact-attention analysis shows the main issue is selector mis-ranking of relevant blocks, not exhausting the fixed budget.
A teacher-forced calibration probe identifies heads that attend to the needle but lose it when mean-pooled key summaries dilute its decisive token.
For InfLLM-V2 and NOSA-8B, the same three blind heads explain much of the multi-key retrieval loss; similar patterns appear in several other sparse-attention methods.
Repairing flagged heads with full attention or a 4-bit scorer preserves the shipped budget and recovers most of the loss without training.
Reported gains include MiniCPM4.1-8B improving from 54.1% to 97.5% at 64K, while selective full attention retains 84–89% of sparse attention’s TTFT savings; MoBA shows many more blind heads.

papers.selection_reason: Diagnoses and repairs block selection in sparse attention for long-context LLMs; directly relevant to efficient attention and long-context models.
papers.title: Lost in a Few Heads: Diagnosing and Repairing Block Selection in Sparse Attention
papers.tldr: A small number of blind attention heads cause most sparse-attention retrieval failures, and selectively repairing them largely restores full-attention accuracy at much of sparse serving’s speed benefit.

papers.abstract: Visual token pruning reduces the inference cost of Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models, but attention-based scores do not directly measure a token's effect on the predicted action. We define action sensitivity as the magnitude of the first-order action change when a token is replaced by its camera's mean token and estimate it for all tokens with a single backward pass. Computing it online is costly: scoring on the full (unpruned) graph needs an extra forward pass at every control step. Scoring on the pruned forward pass is cheaper but causes scoring-graph lock-in: removed tokens lose their direct paths through later layers and tend to receive lower scores, making those locations less likely to return. On replayed observations, even with a random conditioning mask, pruned-graph scoring re-selects 59% of the mask's tokens, versus 6% expected by chance; attention histories show a similar bias. POKE (Probe Offline, Keep Efficiently) computes full-graph action sensitivities offline and distills them into a student with under 0.3M parameters. At inference, the student scores the current observation without backpropagation or previous masks, and score-guided diversity selection retains the tokens. Keeping 32 of 512 visual tokens on LIBERO, POKE achieves 95.2% success on OpenVLA-OFT and 90.8% on $\pi_{0.5}$ at $1.85\times$ and $1.26\times$ speedups, outperforming attention-, diversity-, and distillation-based pruners, with larger margins on LIBERO-Plus.
authors: Jaehyuk Lee, Yeajin Lee, Suhyun Bae, Donghun Lee
bullets: Attention scores poorly reflect how visual tokens affect predicted actions, while online action-sensitivity scoring is computationally expensive and biased by prior pruning.
POKE computes full-graph action sensitivities offline and distills them into a student with fewer than 0.3M parameters.
At inference, the student scores observations without backpropagation or previous masks, and diversity selection retains informative tokens.
Keeping 32 of 512 tokens achieves 95.2% success on OpenVLA-OFT and 90.8% on π0.5, with 1.85× and 1.26× speedups on LIBERO.
The method reports larger gains on LIBERO-Plus than competing attention-, diversity-, and distillation-based pruners.

papers.selection_reason: Action-sensitivity-based visual token pruning for VLA models, combining token efficiency with embodied policy inference.
papers.title: POKE: Probe Offline, Keep Efficiently for Vision-Language-Action Models
papers.tldr: POKE efficiently prunes VLA visual tokens by offline-distilling action sensitivity, achieving strong task performance with substantial inference speedups.

papers.abstract: Diffusion Transformers (DiTs) have achieved strong performance in generation based video editing, but suffer from high inference latency due to the long token sequences formed by conditioning inputs and generated videos. Although training-free sparse attention reduces this cost, existing methods typically apply a fixed retention ratio or a single threshold shared across all tokens. In this work, we view video editing as conditional generation and identify a key insight: attention demand varies significantly both across different key sources (e.g., source videos, reference images, audio, text, and generated videos) and across queries within each source. Motivated by this, we propose QASK-Edit (Query-Adaptive Sparsity over Key Sources for Video Editing), a training-free sparse attention framework that allocates computation independently for each query and key source. Specifically, for each query, QASK-Edit considers both the attention mass and approximation risk of each block. It then evaluates candidate routing thresholds against each key source's risk budget, choosing exact computation or approximations to dynamically adjust sparsity for each query. Extensive experiments on three video editing models demonstrate that QASK-Edit achieves up to $1.46\times$ end-to-end speedup over dense attention pipeline while preserving both editing quality and unedited region fidelity. Furthermore, QASK-Edit generalizes directly to Reference-to-Video generation, delivering up to $1.36\times$ speedup while maintaining generation quality.
authors: Hengrui Liu, Wenbo Xu, Ziqi Sheng, Wei lu
bullets: Addresses high inference latency caused by long conditioning and video token sequences.
Training-free routing adapts computation across sources such as videos, images, audio, text, and generated content.
Balances attention mass and approximation risk to select source-specific thresholds per query.
Achieves up to 1.46× end-to-end speedup in video editing while preserving editing quality and unedited regions.
Also applies to Reference-to-Video generation, achieving up to 1.36× speedup without degrading quality.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Overview of QASK-Edit. The process begins with the generation of summaries for blocks, sub-blocks, and second-level sub-blocks. For each query tile, we independently select a routing threshold for each key source within the risk budget, based on the residual risk introduced by approximate calculations. This routing threshold then determines whether to perform exact or approximate calculations. Finally, we aggregate the contributions of all key sources into a single softmax and output the final result.

Three sampled frames are shown for each source–edited video pair, covering diverse editing tasks such as clothing modification, object replacement, and scene recoloring. The results demonstrate high-quality edits with preserved temporal consistency.

papers.selection_reason: Adaptive sparse attention for efficient video editing; directly addresses attention efficiency and token sparsity.
papers.title: QASK-Edit: Adaptive Sparse Attention Across Queries and Key Sources for Efficient Video Editing
papers.tldr: QASK-Edit accelerates diffusion-transformer video editing by adaptively sparsifying attention for each query and key source while preserving quality and fidelity.

papers.abstract: Visual token pruning improves the efficiency of multimodal large language models (MLLMs) by removing redundant visual tokens, yet the reliability of existing selection signals has not been systematically examined. We analyze token selection under semantics-preserving perturbations and across representative pruning criteria, revealing two limitations. First, attention-based importance shifts non-uniformly under perturbations, so magnitude alone cannot distinguish stable evidence from unstable saliency (local instability). Second, attention- and diversity-based methods select substantially different subsets despite comparable performance, showing that useful evidence is not confined to a unique subset (global inconsistency). These findings motivate reliable token-set construction. We instantiate this perspective in CoRePruner, a training-free framework combining instruction-aware diversity with reliability-aware attention. Across image benchmarks, multiple MLLM architectures, and token budgets, CoRePruner improves performance, especially under aggressive pruning, and remains competitive on video benchmarks. Our results establish reliability as a central consideration in visual token selection.
authors: Chaehee Song, Seokil Ham, KiHyun Seol, Jihyun Lee, Yubin Choi, Changick Kim
bullets: Attention importance can change unevenly under semantics-preserving perturbations, exposing local instability.
Different pruning criteria often select substantially different token subsets despite similar performance, revealing global inconsistency.
CoRePruner is a training-free method using instruction-aware diversity and reliability-aware attention.
It improves performance across image benchmarks, MLLM architectures, and token budgets, particularly under aggressive pruning, while remaining competitive for video.
The study argues that reliability should be a central criterion for visual token selection.

papers.abstract: GPTQ is the de facto standard solver for layer-wise post-training quantization (PTQ) of large language models, yet the solver itself has received less attention than weight preprocessing and cross-layer objectives. We target a bottleneck of GPTQ: its greedy procedure optimizes continuous group scales separately from the assignment of discrete integers. Evaluating each integer candidate with its closed-form optimal scale has been used for per-channel quantization; JointQ extends it to group-wise quantization, where a row's scales are coupled through the Hessian, and applies it to refine the GPTQ solution. Each local-search move changes one integer and recomputes its group's optimal scale in closed form, accounting for the other groups through the full Hessian; all scales are periodically re-solved jointly. The search starts from a row-wise selection among scale-refitted candidates including the GPTQ solution, so unregularized JointQ never has a larger layer-wise calibration error than GPTQ. JointQ preserves the GPTQ output format and is thus a drop-in replacement. Across four models and four settings, JointQ improves six-task average zero-shot accuracy over vanilla GPTQ in 14 of 16 comparisons and perplexity in 12 of 16. The mean accuracy gain increases from 0.0044 in W4G128 to 0.1559 in W3 per-channel, and JointQ also improves average accuracy over GPTQ with MSE-based scale search and activation ordering in all eight per-channel comparisons, though rarely in G128. An ablation shows that JointQ's diagonal Tikhonov regularization mitigates severe W3 per-channel perplexity degradation, so the largest gains are not due to the local search alone. Overall, JointQ's primary empirical benefit is downstream accuracy preservation in challenging low-bit and large-group regimes. Code is available in the OneComp library at https://github.com/FujitsuResearch/OneCompression.
authors: Keiji Kimura, Yuma Ichikawa
bullets: Targets GPTQ’s greedy separation of discrete integer selection from continuous scale optimization.
Uses Hessian-aware local search: each integer update recomputes its group’s closed-form optimal scale, followed by periodic joint scale refinement.
Starts from scale-refitted GPTQ candidates, so unregularized JointQ does not increase layer-wise calibration error relative to GPTQ.
Across four models and four settings, it improves average zero-shot accuracy in 14/16 comparisons and perplexity in 12/16.
Diagonal Tikhonov regularization helps prevent severe W3 per-channel perplexity degradation; JointQ remains a drop-in GPTQ replacement.
