papers.tldr: Visual Token Routing sparsifies screenshot representations for computer-use agents, preserving action performance while substantially reducing visual-token and inference costs.

papers.abstract: Small language models offer a compact basis for shell simulation without executing submitted commands, but full-output decoding requires them to predict recurring utility structure alongside content that varies across executions. We introduce template gap reconstruction (TGR), which supplies reusable output literals interspersed with sentinels to be interleaved with autoregressively generated gaps. A template selector chooses which template to be reconstructed, with the empty template retaining full-output decoding. We construct a template bank from 18.7 million outputs collected across heterogeneous execution environments and train a template selector and five reconstruction models initialized from various small language model checkpoints on a target environment excluded from bank construction. Evaluation demonstrates that TGR improves output edit similarity (O-ES) over full-output decoding (FOD) when the optimal template covers more than 25\% of the template, while performing similarly for lower-coverage outputs. Additionally, TGR outperforms FOD for shorter gap sequences, with O-ES values of 0.964 and 0.812, respectively, while maintaining similar performance for longer sequences. TGR reduces the number of tokens generated by 26.3--38.3\% across used tokenizer families. These results support using a reusable output structure as a practical design choice for small shell simulators, improving response fidelity and shortening generation targets while keeping template selection and residual prediction central to response quality.
authors: Jarrod Ragsdale, Rajendra Boppana
bullets: Addresses the difficulty of predicting recurring shell-output structure alongside execution-specific content without running commands.
Provides reusable output templates with sentinels; the model autoregressively generates only the missing gaps.
A template selector chooses a reconstruction template, while an empty template preserves full-output decoding.
Improves output edit similarity when templates cover more than 25% of the output and performs similarly at lower coverage.
Outperforms full-output decoding on shorter gap sequences, with O-ES of 0.964 versus 0.812, while maintaining similar performance on longer sequences.

papers.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models map camera observations and language instructions to robot actions. However, their large backbones and repeated action generation can make inference take longer than the robot's real-time requirements for its next action. To reduce the load of VLA computations, researchers have proposed multiple optimization approaches, including quantization and pruning. These optimizations can be combined with other general optimizations such as better kernel compilation or using CUDA graphs instead of the eager mode. However, most of these optimization results are usually reported on a single GPU type, typically for a few VLA models, with no analysis of what the real bottlenecks are for a model on a particular hardware or how these optimizations would generalize beyond the reported results. In this paper, we provide a comprehensive measurement study of seven families of inference optimization methods, from CUDA graphs and compilation to token pruning and quantization, on seven state-of-the-art VLAs evaluated on four GPU families ranging from a datacenter H100 to an embedded Jetson Thor. We analyse how CPU launch overhead, memory bandwidth, and kernel efficiency jointly shape optimization gains, and how applying one method changes the benefit of another. From this analysis, we derive VLA-Triage, guidelines for stacking optimizations under latency budgets. The guidelines identify which stages can provide the required savings and which combinations need testing in the deployed execution mode.
authors: Muhammad Danish Waseem, Ahmed Ali-Eldin Hassan
bullets: Evaluates seven inference-optimization families across seven VLAs and four GPU families, from H100 to Jetson Thor.
Analyzes the roles of CPU launch overhead, memory bandwidth, and kernel efficiency in determining optimization gains.
Shows that optimization benefits and interactions depend on the model, hardware, and deployed execution mode.
Introduces VLA-Triage, guidelines for selecting and stacking optimizations under latency budgets.

papers.title: Where Is VLA Inference Time Spent? Bottlenecks and Optimization Interactions Across GPUs
papers.tldr: A cross-GPU study identifies where VLA inference time is spent and provides guidelines for combining optimizations to meet robot latency requirements.

papers.abstract: Feed-forward 3D Gaussian Splatting enables efficient generalizable novel view synthesis, but existing pixel-aligned methods often generate highly redundant Gaussian primitives, causing the final representation size and rendering cost to grow rapidly with image resolution and the number of input views. We propose BudgetSplat, a budget-controllable feed-forward framework that adapts the final Gaussian representation to a user-specified preservation ratio. Rather than treating compaction as simple importance ranking, we formulate it as a joint problem of importance estimation, spatial coverage, and cross-view redundancy. A single trained model supports varying numbers of context views and multiple test-time budgets without per-budget retraining or per-scene compression. To realize this formulation, Intra-Cross Mask Supervision provides structure-, coverage-, and redundancy-aware guidance for learning Gaussian importance, while budget-conditioned feature modulation adapts Gaussian opacity and attributes to the requested preservation ratio. Coverage-Aware Budget Selection further combines patch-wise pre-selection, view-wise opacity ranking, and 3D redundancy suppression to construct compact yet spatially distributed Gaussian representations. Experiments on indoor reconstruction and cross-dataset generalization demonstrate consistent quality--size trade-offs across different input view counts and preservation ratios, substantially reducing final representation storage and rendering cost while preserving rendering quality.
authors: Yuxi Hu, Jun Zhang, Wei Mao, Yuchen Rao, Friedrich Fraundorfer
bullets: Addresses redundant Gaussian primitives that make representation size and rendering cost grow with image resolution and input views.
Jointly models Gaussian importance, spatial coverage, and cross-view redundancy rather than relying on simple importance ranking.
Uses Intra-Cross Mask Supervision and budget-conditioned feature modulation to adapt Gaussian attributes to different preservation ratios.
Coverage-Aware Budget Selection combines patch pre-selection, view-wise opacity ranking, and 3D redundancy suppression.
Experiments show consistent quality–size trade-offs across varying input views and budgets, without per-budget retraining or per-scene compression.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Overview of BudgetSplat. (A) Given 𝑁 posed context images, a pixel-aligned reconstruction backbone estimates dense geometry and base Gaussian features. (B) During training, Intra-Cross Mask Supervision constructs pseudo importance targets that preserve high-frequency structures, maintain sparse coverage in low-frequency regions, and down-weight redundant cross-view observations. (C) Budget-Conditioned Feature Modulation injects the user-specified preservation ratio 𝜌 into the base Gaussian features before parameter prediction, allowing the predicted opacity and Gaussian attributes to adapt to the requested budget. (D) Coverage-Aware Budget Selection combines patch-wise pre-selection, view-wise global opacity ranking, and 3D redundancy suppression to retain a compact and spatially distributed Gaussian representation. A single trained model supports arbitrary test-time preservation ratios 𝜌 ∈ (0, 1] without retraining.

papers.abstract: Large vision-language models (LVLMs) have recently been extended to handle multiple input images, but this extension dramatically increases the visual token budget, making visual-token pruning not merely an efficiency option but a practical necessity. Existing visual-token pruning methods, primarily designed for the single-image setting, rely on attention-derived saliency signals to estimate per-token importance. However, this attention-centric design transfers poorly to the multi-image regime: it causes substantial performance degradation on multi-image benchmarks, suffers from strong positional bias, and loses discriminative attention signals as the number of input images increases. To test whether attention-selected tokens are truly important for multi-image reasoning, we conduct two complementary causal probes Leave-One-In and Leave-One-Deletion, which measure token importance by restoring individual tokens to a zeroed visual sequence or removing them from the full sequence. Attention-based pruners provide only marginal gains over random selection, showing that attention is a weak proxy for visual-token importance in multi-image reasoning. Motivated by this gap, we propose Relation and Information Aware Pruning (RI-Prune), a training-free, attention-free pre-decoder selector for multi-image visual token pruning. RI-Prune scores each visual token using a z-normalized combination of three signals computed from projector outputs: query relevance, cross-image correspondence with compact per-image prototypes, and intra image representativeness. By integrating these signals, RI-Prune performs balanced per-image Top-K selection to preserve information across input images. Across multiple multi-image benchmarks and three LVLM backbones, RI-Prune achieves a stronger trade-off between token reduction and task performance than prior pruning methods, particularly under aggressive token budgets.
authors: Dongjin Lee, Eunju Lee, Jinhee Jang, Yoonji Lee, Youngbin Kim
bullets: Multi-image inputs greatly increase visual-token budgets, making pruning necessary for practical LVLM inference.
Attention-based pruning transfers poorly to multi-image reasoning due to positional bias and weakening attention signals as image count grows.
Causal Leave-One-In and Leave-One-Deletion probes show attention-selected tokens are only marginally better than random selections.
RI-Prune is a training-free, attention-free pre-decoder selector using three z-normalized projector-output signals.
Balanced per-image Top-K selection preserves information across images and yields a better token-reduction/task-performance trade-off, especially at aggressive budgets.

Figure 4: Qualitative visualization of visual token pruning on MUIRBench [34]. Bright regions indicate retained visual tokens. Colored boxes denote question-relevant regions: green indicates successful preservation, red indicates pruning of critical information, and orange indicates ambiguous preservation that ultimately leads to an incorrect prediction. Figure 1: Failure modes of attention-based visual token pruning in multi-image LVLMs. (a) Single-image pruning methods retain high performance on single-image benchmarks but degrade sharply on multi-image benchmarks, showing poor transfer to multi-image reasoning. (b) Query attention becomes unreliable across images: it exhibits positional bias and becomes increasingly non-discriminative as the number of input images grows. (c) CLS-based saliency selects tokens with weaker query alignment than query-driven attention, suggesting that CLS attention is less effective at preserving question-relevant visual evidence.

papers.title: RI-Prune: Relation and Information Aware Visual Token Pruning for Multi-Image Vision-Language Models
papers.tldr: RI-Prune improves multi-image LVLM efficiency by selecting visual tokens using relevance, cross-image relations, and within-image representativeness instead of attention alone.

papers.abstract: KV cache eviction is not merely a token-ranking problem: the workspace retained for generating eviction queries also determines the quality of those queries. Consequently, an early workspace error can distort later query observations and reinforce an incorrect final eviction decision, particularly when evidence is dispersed across a long context. We present EchoKV, which discovers and addresses this failure mode with iterative correction. It initializes a feedback-compatible bootstrap workspace using proposals at future decode positions, then uses early decode-generated queries to recover the workspace before the remaining lookahead steps. It uses the same number of workspace forward passes as LAQ while adding a tensor re-scoring operation for workspace repair. On LongBench (16 tasks, Mistral-7B-Instruct-v0.2 and Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct), EchoKV shows notable improvements over LAQ on several tasks requiring dispersed evidence, including multi-hop cross-document QA and long single-document comprehension. Across budgets and backbones, EchoKV selectively improves evidence-intensive tasks while maintaining comparable performance on the remaining LongBench subsets. These results identify query--workspace coupling as a practical failure mode of query-driven KV eviction.
authors: JianKun Zou, Tongtong Yuan
bullets: Problem: Early workspace errors can corrupt later queries and reinforce incorrect eviction decisions.
Method: Bootstrap a feedback-compatible workspace, use early decode queries to recover it, then continue lookahead-based eviction.
Efficiency: Matches LAQ’s number of workspace forward passes and adds tensor re-scoring for workspace repair.
Results: Improves several LongBench evidence-intensive tasks, including multi-hop cross-document QA and long-document comprehension, across budgets and two model backbones.
Scope: Gains are selective, while performance remains comparable on other LongBench subsets.

figures.caption: Figure 1: EchoKV overview. papers.title: EchoKV: Self-Corrective KV Cache Eviction via Iterative Query Feedback

papers.abstract: Vision Transformers (ViTs) are bottlenecked by the length of their input token sequence. Standard patchification fixes this length with a single patch size applied across the image, regardless of regional content. Prior work on adaptive patch sizing reduces token count by assigning coarser patches to visually simple regions, but relies on noisy pixel-level heuristics such as local entropy to make patchification decisions. We argue that this compute allocation should be grounded in the model's interpretation of task relevant information, not in raw pixel statistics. We introduce Split Policy Learned Image Tokenization which learns to allocate token resolution based on what the model finds meaningful, producing shorter token sequences that are better matched to task-relevant content. SPLIT matches the accuracy of full-resolution ViT classification baselines while using 30% fewer tokens. The same gains hold on dense prediction: SPLIT achieves competitive accuracy on COCO and ADE20K, demonstrating that semantically aligned patchification generalises well beyond classification.
authors: Aditya Gupta, Jean Sebastien Dandurand, Kai Qiu, Rohan Choudhury, Laszlo A. Jeni
bullets: Standard fixed-size patchification ignores regional complexity and creates unnecessarily long sequences.
SPLIT replaces pixel-level heuristics with a learned hierarchical patch-splitting policy guided by the model’s interpretation.
It matches full-resolution ViT classification accuracy while using 30% fewer tokens.
The approach also delivers competitive dense-prediction accuracy on COCO and ADE20K.
The abstract focuses on image classification and dense prediction; broader scope is not established.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of SPLIT. An input image is first divided into coarse patches. A decision network then performs S refinement stages, deciding whether to split each parent patch into its children or keep it as a single token. The example uses two splitting stages, yielding a mixed-resolution token sequence. For each parent-child group, a lightweight cross-attention module pools the four child embeddings with the parent embedding as the query. The pooled summary is concatenated with the parent embedding and passed to a two-layer MLP to predict the split probability pi.

Figure 1: Split Policy Learned Image Tokenization. SPLIT is an adaptive patchification framework that learns to allocate fine tokens to semantically important regions and coarse tokens to homogeneous ones, accelerating ViT inference without sacrificing accuracy.
Figure 5: Comparison of our method against APT.
Figure 7: Patch allocation comparison. APT (middle) over-tokenizes high-entropy textures regardless of their semantic content, while SPLIT (bottom) concentrates fine tokens around objects.

Figure 6: Adaptive λ more reliably controls the token budget than fixed-λ baselines. Left: percent tokens used during training, with the dashed line indicating the 50% target. Right: absolute deviation from the target token budget on train and validation sets.

Figure 9: Object detection qualitative comparison (Vanilla vs Ours). We compare fixed-grid ViT inference (Vanilla) against our learned multi-stage patch splitting method. For each example, we visualize the patch assignment map and the corresponding detection output. Our method allocates finer patches to detail-heavy regions while preserving detection quality.

Figure 10: Semantic segmentation qualitative comparison (Vanilla vs Ours). We compare fixedgrid ViT inference (Vanilla) against our learned multi-stage patch splitting method. For each example, we visualize the patch assignment map and the corresponding segmentation output. Our method allocates finer patches to detail-heavy regions while preserving segmentation quality.
Figure 8: Splitting decision at different token budgets Visualizing the patch splitting decisions at various token budgets shows how the model progressively prioritizes patches based on content.

papers.abstract: Long-horizon video generation is increasingly moving toward autoregressive rollout, where each newly generated segment becomes part of the evidence used for future prediction. Recent causal decoders, long-context training, and KV-cache mechanisms have extended feasible duration, but most inference pipelines still decide the visible past implicitly through recent windows, compressed caches, or external memory. This raises a direct question: \textbf{can the choice of which past frames or segments to show to the decoder be treated as an explicit test-time decision?} We answer this question with \textsc{ReCR}, a training-free method that formulates autoregressive video decoding as representation-guided context rewriting. At each step, \textsc{ReCR} builds a selected visible context from the generated history by using internal decoder representations to favor context units that match the global rollout state, avoid redundancy with the recent continuation, preserve temporal boundary coverage, and widen the range of spatial layouts in view. The selected units are then mapped onto a compact causal axis before decoding the next block. Across long-horizon text-to-video benchmarks, \textsc{ReCR} consistently improves multiple autoregressive backbones under matched visible-token budgets. Empirical analyses such as representation-space diagnostics and transition-count prompt switching further show that improving what remains visible is an effective path toward more stable long-video decoding.
authors: Lixuan He, Jihyeon Je, Yang You, Leonidas Guibas
bullets: Frames or segments shown to the decoder are treated as an explicit test-time selection decision.
The training-free method uses internal representations to select globally relevant, nonredundant context.
It preserves temporal boundary coverage and increases the diversity of visible spatial layouts.
Selected context units are placed on a compact causal axis before generating the next video block.
Across long-horizon text-to-video benchmarks, ReCR improves multiple autoregressive backbones under matched visible-token budgets.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of the ReCR framework. Instead of exposing the full generated history or a fixed recent window, ReCR scores context units with unit-level representations and selects a compact visible context. At most one spatial-range exchange, not drawn here, then refines the selection (Sec. 3.2). The selected context is then temporally reindexed onto a compact causal axis before being passed to the causal video decoder.

papers.abstract: Attention is known to be sparse in vision transformers. In particular, we analyze the unequal relevance of attention-matrix columns to the final computation and show that this phenomenon becomes increasingly pronounced with network depth. This can be interpreted as saying that tokens have an absolute importance for the attention process, independently of queries. Inspired by this, we propose a reformulation of the attention formula that makes this phenomenon explicit by adding an input-dependent bias to the query-key dot product. We show that this new term gives each token a scalar value indicating its anticipated influence on other tokens during the attention process, and can thus serve as a proxy for pruning attention maps. Across multiple transformer model sizes, this allows us to substantially reduce the computational cost of attention, in terms of both FLOPs and inference latency, while retaining most of the original classification accuracy. We publicly released the code and models at https://github.com/EIDOSLAB/AttentionWithBias.
authors: Charles Herr, Gabriele Spadaro, Enzo Tartaglione
bullets: Attention-matrix columns contribute unequally to the final computation, with this imbalance increasing at greater network depth.
The method adds an input-dependent bias to query–key dot products to estimate each token’s anticipated influence on others.
These scalar token scores act as a proxy for pruning attention maps.
Across multiple transformer sizes, pruning substantially reduces attention FLOPs and inference latency while retaining most classification accuracy.
Code and models are publicly released.

papers.abstract: Large Vision-Language Models (LVLMs) often process hundreds or thousands of visual tokens, resulting in substantial computational and memory overhead during inference. Existing training-free pruning methods typically estimate token importance using language-model attention, visual attention, or feature similarity. However, these methods treat visual tokens with uniform criteria and overlook that tokens may serve different roles during visual encoding. In this work, we investigate the evolution of visual token roles in LVLMs and observe that tokens progressively transition from local detail carriers to globally referenced representatives as encoding proceeds. Based on this observation, we propose BtsPruner, a training-free role-aware visual token pruning framework that preserves complementary token roles under a fixed budget. Specifically, BtsPruner first identifies the token-role transition point based on the evolution of attention concentration. It then discovers globally referenced representatives from later encoding stages and recursively retrieves local detail tokens from earlier stages to recover complementary fine-grained evidence. Extensive experiments across LLaVA-1.5, LLaVA-NeXT, Qwen-VL, InternVL, and CogVLM demonstrate that BtsPruner achieves superior performance retention under aggressive token reduction. On LLaVA-1.5-7B, BtsPruner preserves 91.6% of the dense model's performance using only 32 of 576 visual tokens (5.6%). In the high-resolution LLaVA-NeXT-7B setting, it achieves up to a 5.95x CUDA-latency speedup.
authors: Zihao Qi, Zhibo Zhang, Miaoxin Zhang, Jincheng Cai, Zengqiang Yan
bullets: LVLM inference is costly because it processes hundreds or thousands of visual tokens.
The method observes that tokens evolve from local detail carriers to globally referenced representatives during encoding.
It identifies this role-transition point, selects global representatives from later stages, and recursively retrieves complementary local tokens from earlier stages.
Across multiple LVLMs, it retains strong performance under substantial token reduction.
On LLaVA-1.5-7B, it retains 91.6% of dense-model performance with 32/576 tokens; on LLaVA-NeXT-7B, it provides up to 5.95× CUDA-latency speedup.

papers.abstract: We present a spatial-memory system that enables optical see-through AR glasses to recall earlier physical encounters. The dual-camera prototype combines hierarchical visual acquisition with source-linked storage and staged retrieval. Quality screen-ing, global and regional appearance novelty, and temporal support select monochrome observations for detailed RGB cap-ture. Semantic observations retain links to their source images, allowing retrieval to answer indexed historical questions direct-ly or inspect visual details omitted from scene descriptions. The architecture separates capture acceptance, interpretation out-come, and support for a particular question. This distinction motivates two core control mechanisms: bounded reassessment of familiar views when earlier processing leaves an evidence gap, and retention guided by source dependencies. In a 131.35 s egocentric replay, the implemented acquisition policy selected six RGB views from 648 monitoring observations, while feature extraction ran on 97.7% of observations. These results demon-strate selective RGB acquisition and identify frequent local inference as a remaining cost. Exposure duration and cross-view timing further constrain the evidence preserved from se-lected encounters. The system provides a practical acquisition-to-recall architecture for persistent AR assistance, with explicit boundaries between captured evidence, indexed interpretations, and supported historical claims.
authors: Tianxing Zhu, Dan Huang
bullets: Addresses persistent AR assistance when historical questions require visual evidence from earlier encounters.
Uses hierarchical acquisition: quality, novelty, and temporal cues select monochrome observations for detailed RGB capture.
Links semantic observations to source images and separates capture acceptance, interpretation, and question-specific support.
Introduces bounded reassessment of familiar views and source-dependency-guided retention.

papers.abstract: Effective world modeling requires compressing salient history information that facilitates future prediction. However, most existing approaches inherit tokenization and conditioning mechanisms from video generation, where objectives are centered around perceptual realism rather than predictive utility. This discrepancy limits the world model's effectiveness, especially in environments dominated by visual nuisances or task-irrelevant background details. To this end, we introduce Compression Forcing (CF), a general framework that aligns history compression with the predictive objective of world modeling. Compression Forcing features Dynamics-Aware Tokenization (DAT), a novel tokenization method that compresses history observations into a sequence ordered by decreasing dynamics saliency. Built on a diffusion backbone, this structure enables Hierarchical History Guidance (HG-H), allowing selective amplification of dynamics-salient information during inference. Extensive experiments across various environments demonstrate improved prediction fidelity, physical realism, and downstream decision-making performance, establishing Compression Forcing as a highly flexible and effective approach for world modeling.
authors: Siqiao Huang, Partha Kaushik, Michael Chen, Hengkai Pan, Kaiwen Geng, Omar Chehab, Fernando Moreno-Pino, Max Simchowitz
bullets: Addresses the mismatch between video-generation tokenization and world-modeling objectives, particularly under visual nuisances.
Introduces Dynamics-Aware Tokenization, which orders compressed history tokens by decreasing dynamics saliency.
Uses Hierarchical History Guidance with a diffusion backbone to selectively amplify salient information during inference.
Experiments across varied environments report better prediction fidelity, physical realism, and downstream decision-making.
Scope: designed for environments where task-irrelevant visual details can hinder predictive modeling.

papers.abstract: Reasoning substantially improves language models' ability to solve difficult problems, but long reasoning traces make these gains expensive. Efficient reasoning should express useful analysis in fewer tokens by reducing repetition and text that adds little value to solving the problem. Progress in proprietary models motivates this goal, yet their hidden scratchpads limit direct study of how it is achieved. We investigate whether open-weight models can generate less verbose reasoning by changing the form of their own earlier thoughts, without retraining. Our intervention rewrites prior reasoning into compact state records before pending tool results are revealed, then compares continuations from original and compact histories. Across the tested models, accepted compact histories usually shorten future reasoning; a coding case study also shows less repeated verification after a shared candidate solution. In software-agent deployments, compaction can reduce total spending, although task quality and rewrite-inclusive time depend on the target and compressor. These findings identify reasoning history as one way to reduce future reasoning-token use and motivate model-specific compaction policies evaluated for both efficiency and retained capability.
authors: Anton Hristov
bullets: Long reasoning traces improve problem-solving but can be expensive due to repetition and low-value text.
The study compacts earlier reasoning before pending tool results are revealed, then compares generation from original versus rewritten histories without retraining.
Across tested models, accepted compact histories generally shortened subsequent reasoning; a coding case showed less repeated verification.
Software-agent deployments achieved lower total spending, but task quality and rewrite-inclusive time varied by target and compressor.
The results motivate model-specific compaction policies that balance efficiency with retained capability.

papers.abstract: Non-injective mappings in neural networks map distinct inputs to the same representation, thereby implicitly inducing equivalence relations in the input space. However, the input differences eliminated by these mappings may still be required by downstream tasks, creating a mismatch between operator-induced indistinguishability and task-required distinctions. For non-injective linear operators realized in the current forward pass, their null spaces exactly characterize these invisible input variations. We propose Task-Relevant Null-Space Residuals (NSR), a general residual framework for non-injective linear mappings. NSR combines null-space component extraction from pre-mapping representations, member-level encoding and gating, and application-specific integration to exploit potentially task-relevant information under downstream supervision while preserving the original aggregation or merging rules. We evaluate NSR in two structurally different settings: token merging and graph aggregation. In token merging, NSR achieves higher semantic segmentation performance than the corresponding compressed baselines in 34 out of 36 evaluated configurations, with a maximum observed gain of 31.51 mIoU points under strong compression. In graph aggregation, NSR achieves 100% training accuracy on Tree-NeighborsMatch at depths d=2--6 across three backbones, alongside gains on heterophilic node classification and molecular graph regression. Together, these results support null-space residuals as a practical complement to non-injective linear mappings, enabling downstream models to learn from input distinctions invisible in the original operator's output.
authors: Bizu Feng
Zhimu Yang
Shuming Wang
Yuan Cheng
Shaode Yu
Xiaojun Qian

bullets: Non-injective mappings collapse distinct inputs, potentially removing distinctions needed by downstream tasks.

For token merging, NSR outperforms compressed baselines in 34 of 36 configurations, with a maximum gain of 31.51 mIoU points.
For graph aggregation, it reaches 100% training accuracy on Tree-NeighborsMatch at depths 2–6 across three backbones and improves other graph tasks.

papers.abstract: In real-world deployments, large language model (LLM) systems are increasingly evolving from single-model invocation toward heterogeneous deployments in which different models are dynamically invoked for inference. When the same context is reused across models, however, each newly selected target model typically has to process it again, repeatedly incurring substantial computational costs. Therefore, we propose ACCT (Asymmetric Cross-LLM Context Transfer), which targets KV cache transfer between models of different scales within the same model family. ACCT transforms the KV cache produced by a source model into sparse KV states that can be directly consumed by a target model, thereby enabling cross-model reuse of context computation and decoupling context computation from downstream inference. ACCT consists of three lightweight components: the Cartographer identifies query-relevant context tokens for each target layer and KV head; the Allocator determines how many context tokens each target layer and KV head retains under a shared total KV budget; and the Compiler transforms selected source KV into sparse target KV. The target model can therefore perform inference using the transferred KV without reprocessing the original context. We evaluate ACCT in two complementary settings comprising five general-capability benchmarks and six highly context-dependent tasks. Experiments show that ACCT matches or exceeds the target model's original inference performance even when reducing the KV cache size by 75%. At a context length of approximately 19K tokens, ACCT's KV conversion achieves a 6.5-21.2 times speedup over target context prefill. These results demonstrate the feasibility of transferring context computation across models under a limited KV budget.
authors: Yuzhe Liu, Haolin Tian, Tonghan Wang
bullets: Addresses the cost of recomputing shared context when dynamically switching among heterogeneous LLMs.

Evaluated on five general-capability benchmarks and six context-dependent tasks.

papers.abstract: The quadratic scaling of attention is a fundamental bottleneck limiting the long-context capabilities of large language models (LLMs). A variety of approaches have attempted to circumvent this, but they either fail to match attention's expressiveness (e.g., sliding-window or linear attention variants with fixed-size state) or only achieve constant-factor speedups (e.g., sparse attention methods whose indexers themselves scale quadratically). In this paper, we derive an asymptotically subquadratic sparse attention method based on a hierarchical, tree-structured indexer, which we call Zyphra Hierarchical Attention (ZHA). ZHA constructs a tree of recursively compressed key summaries over the KV cache, which future queries traverse from the top down to retrieve a sparse subset of keys. Crucially, by iteratively growing the tree's depth, the total cost including routing and final attention grows sublinearly in sequence length, resulting in overall subquadratic (but superlinear) scaling for attention. We demonstrate that ZHA can be cheaply applied to existing pretrained models with only a short KL distillation training stage over a few billion tokens, and maintains performance on long-context retrieval and challenging reasoning, mathematical, and agentic coding evaluation tasks. Moreover, we show that our method is highly robust to tree geometry including very deep trees of up to 6 levels. Finally, we develop a detailed performance model and show that our approach scales subquadratically, dramatically outperforms competing methods beyond 1 million context, and ultimately has the potential to extend effective context windows to the hundreds of millions or billions of tokens.
authors: Leon Lufkin, Cutter Dawes, Alexander Speicher, Kamesh Krishnamurthy, Tom\'as Figliolia, Beren Millidge
bullets: Addresses quadratic attention cost, which limits long-context scaling.
Builds a hierarchical tree of compressed key summaries that queries traverse to select sparse keys.
Joint routing and attention cost grows subquadratically—sublinear in sequence length for the relevant computation, but still superlinear overall.
Can be added to pretrained models using a short KL-distillation stage and maintains long-context retrieval, reasoning, math, and coding performance.
The authors report strong scaling beyond 1 million tokens and potential context windows of hundreds of millions to billions of tokens; performance depends on the method’s tree-based indexing scope.

figures.caption: Figure 3: Overview of the ZHA architecture: (a) tree construction and (b) sparse routing. During tree construction, for each chunk of contiguous key nodes, we construct a compressed key node at the higher level by an attention-weighted sum of the keys, where the attention is computed with respect to the learned reference queries. In practice, we use multiple reference queries and store the key nodes for each in parallel. This process continues recursively with higher level key nodes being constructed from the summaries of lower levels. During routing, we start at the top of the tree and compute dot-product similarity scores between our query and the key nodes of that level. We select the set of nodes to expand using top-p, and then recursively descend the tree until we reach the leaf nodes corresponding to raw KV cache entries. The union of all the leaves we reach defines the sparse KV cache subset that we dispatch to the main attention.

Importantly, we have not empirically validated the scaling at these ultra-long context lengths due to the lack of existing LLMs which can operate at these contexts. Because of this, while we can obtain subquadratic latency, it is unclear to what extent reasoning and retrieval performance degrades at the level of depths required for these ultra-long contexts. papers.abstract: The bottleneck of attention mechanisms, which are the fundamental building block of modern language models, is their quadratic complexity in terms of context size. There has thus been an increasing interest in the compression of the context, also called KV-cache compression. In this article, we consider the problem of compressing the context of attention mechanisms by first formulating it in the Hilbert space associated with its kernel. In this formalism, attention can be represented as the ratio of two linear maps whose interpolant is also the ratio of interpolants, this allows us to consider the interpolation of the linear maps directly. We thus introduce two novel KV-cache compression methods which we call GAIM and Q-DAIM, based on the Generalized Empirical Interpolation Method (GEIM) and the Q-Discrete Empirical Interpolation Method (Q-DEIM), respectively. As the cost of these methods is quadratic in terms of context length, we propose surrogate models based on the Taylor series, the Performer and the Random Fourier Features method which allow the compression to be done in linear time. Finally, we extend this result to the streaming attention setting, providing new methods which allow one to penalize the selection of interpolation nodes based on the previously interpolated context and to update the previous interpolation based on new information. We then provide numerical results on the convergence of the residuals and the output error in future queries and preliminary results on the LongBench-E benchmark showing performance comparable to the state-of-the-art methods. These experiments suggest that the range revealed by our Q-DAIM method could help identify where information is concentrated in the KV cache, thus enabling an efficient compression.
authors: Michel Fabrice Serret, Laura Grigori
bullets: Addresses the quadratic cost of attention with increasing context length by compressing the KV cache.
Formulates attention in a kernel-associated Hilbert space, representing it as a ratio of linear maps whose interpolants can be compressed directly.
Proposes GAIM and Q-DAIM methods based on GEIM and Q-DEIM interpolation techniques.
Uses Taylor-series, Performer, and Random Fourier Features surrogates to reduce compression cost from quadratic to linear time, and extends the approach to streaming attention.

Numerical experiments evaluate residual and future-query output errors; preliminary LongBench-E results show performance comparable to existing methods, while suggesting Q-DAIM can reveal where KV-cache information is concentrated.

papers.abstract: Pixel-space generative Transformers typically use one token per image patch, so capturing finer detail requires more tokens and makes global attention increasingly expensive. We observe that finer detail does not necessarily require more global communication: low-frequency structure benefits from global exchange, while high-frequency detail can be modeled locally. Based on this insight, we introduce SpecSlot, a pixel-space rectified-flow Transformer that decouples output detail from the length of the global attention sequence. SpecSlot expands each spatial anchor into multiple slots, each assigned a disjoint band of DCT coefficients; this separates anchor density from spectral subdivision. Only the lowest-frequency slot from each anchor participates in global attention, while all slots interact locally. This allows the model to increase spectral detail without enlarging the global sequence. A spatial head further adds a local correction to the spectral prediction, while the generative state, target, and loss remain in pixel space. On ImageNet-256, SpecSlot achieves a comparable final FID to a FLOPs-matched JiT control while converging faster. On ImageNet-512, it improves FID by 2.84 over the control with 3.9% fewer FLOPs, and comes within only 0.69 FID of JiT-B/16 at 38.2% lower cost. On text-to-image generation, SpecSlot surpasses JiT-B/8 on DPG-Bench by 1.06 at 40.6% lower forward cost.
authors: Jiongfan Yang, Weichen Fan, Haiwen Diao, Zhongang Cai, Ziwei Liu
bullets: Global attention captures low-frequency structure, while high-frequency detail is modeled locally.

On ImageNet-512, SpecSlot improves FID by 2.84 with 3.9% fewer FLOPs than a matched JiT control.
It also approaches JiT-B/16 at 38.2% lower cost and surpasses JiT-B/8 on DPG-Bench at 40.6% lower forward cost.

papers.abstract: Agents powered by large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated remarkable progress in solving complex reasoning tasks. However, LLM agents often falter on long-horizon tasks due to cognitive overload, as their working memory becomes cluttered with expanding and irrelevant information, which dilutes their attention and hinders effective planning and reasoning. To mitigate this challenge, we introduce Cognitive Resource Self-Allocation (CORAL), a novel reasoning paradigm that empowers agents to proactively optimize their context. Implemented as an agent-callable working memory management toolset, CORAL allows an agent to checkpoint its task progress and verified facts, and adaptively initiate a new problem-solving episode by resetting cluttered context while preserving only the checkpointed information, enabling it to resume reasoning from a clean state. We further enhance the agent's checkpointing capabilities using a Multi-episode Agentic Reinforced Policy Optimization algorithm. On the GAIA benchmark, CORAL with an 8B model achieves 42.8% average accuracy, with particularly strong gains on the most challenging long-horizon tasks (Level 2 and Level 3). Crucially, these gains come at a substantially lower inference cost: CORAL consumes 6-7$\times$ fewer input tokens than a ReAct agent. It also generalizes to multi-hop Knowledge QA benchmarks and to the considerably harder BrowseComp, where it improves a strong proprietary agent by 8.0 points.
authors: Zheng Zhu, Xiaozhuan Liang, Xi Chen, Bei Yu, Jiaya Jia
bullets: Long-horizon agents can suffer from cognitive overload as irrelevant context accumulates and disrupts planning.

A Multi-episode Agentic Reinforced Policy Optimization algorithm improves the agent’s checkpointing decisions.
On GAIA, an 8B model with CORAL reaches 42.8% average accuracy, with especially strong gains on difficult Level 2 and Level 3 tasks.
CORAL uses 6–7× fewer input tokens than ReAct and also improves performance on multi-hop Knowledge QA and BrowseComp.

One context accumulates N ReAct blocks (thought, action, observation) above the system prompt and user task, and nothing is ever removed. Bottom (CORAL). The same blocks are interleaved with two agent-callable tools. Memory Management (MM) writes into the persistent MEMORY panel below the trace, holding task progress (the plan, each sub-goal pending or completed) and verified facts, so that panel evolves while the raw trace only grows. Context Optimization (CO), the vertical bar, ends the current episode: everything to its left is discarded and the next episode restarts from only the system prompt, the user task, and the current panel. A trajectory is thus a sequence of episodes (here 0–3).

papers.abstract: Multi-turn conversations with multimodal large language models (MLLMs) reuse input context, but long multimodal inputs increase time to first token (TTFT). Query-aware hard pruning reduces prefill tokens but permanently excludes information that later questions may require. We propose Raincheck, a framework for deferred multimodal prefill that decouples initial token selection from later information availability. An existing pruning method selects tokens for initial prefill; Raincheck preserves and progressively prefills unselected tokens in source order using unused compute capacity during decode. Unfinished prefill continues after answer return during available scheduling gaps. Attention visibility control and affine state mapping enable context updates after generation begins in full-attention and hybrid recurrent models. Prefill-decode fusion reduces repeated weight reads. We evaluate Qwen3-VL-8B and Qwen3.5-9B with 30% initial multimodal-token retention. Across both models and four pruning methods, Raincheck recovers on average 77.7% and 60.4% of the quality lost to matched hard pruning on MultiVerse and ConvBench, respectively. On MultiVerse, the SGLang implementation reduces mean first-turn TTFT by up to 24.1% relative to full prefill, with less than 0.5% increase in mean time per output token (TPOT).

papers.abstract: Unified Multimodal Models (UMMs) enable powerful multi-image synthesis but incur substantial computation from long visual contexts. While token pruning offers a direct route to accelerating inference, existing methods are primarily adapted from understanding tasks, suffering from insufficient reference image exploration, confused conditional guidance, and pooling-induced ambiguity that degrades generation quality. To address these issues, we propose CATP, the first training-free context-compression method tailored to UMM generation, which \textbf{C}alibrates the discrepancies of general \textbf{A}ttention-based \textbf{T}oken \textbf{P}runing for better quality-efficiency trade-off. Concretely, building on independent layer-wise pruning during denoising, we introduce Guidance-Consistent Pruning (GCP) to synchronize pruning decisions across conditioning branches, and a Taylor-Calibrated Attention Metric (TCAM) that derives a theoretically grounded second-order correction for pooling-induced bias. In addition, a Fast Scoring Operator (FSO) fuses the calibration into tiled online Softmax to reduce pruning cost. Extensive experiments across representative UMMs and benchmarks demonstrate that CATP consistently outperforms state-of-the-art token-reduction methods, achieving up to 2.09$\times$ attention-core speedup.
authors: Zimeng Wu, Qijian Tian, Penghui Du, Changqian Yu, Jiaxin Chen, Yunhong Wang
bullets: Targets the high computation cost of long visual contexts in UMM generation.
Introduces Guidance-Consistent Pruning to align pruning decisions across conditioning branches.
Uses a Taylor-Calibrated Attention Metric to correct pooling-induced pruning bias.
Adds a Fast Scoring Operator that integrates calibration into tiled online Softmax for lower pruning overhead.
Experiments across UMMs and benchmarks report up to 2.09× attention-core speedup and consistent gains over prior token-reduction methods.

papers.abstract: Large vision-language models (LVLMs) represent images and videos as long visual-token sequences, substantially increasing inference costs. These costs motivate visual-token pruning, whose effectiveness depends on both what signal is used for selection and when that signal becomes available. Our analysis reveals complementary limitations: visual-side [CLS] attention produces scattered, background-biased selections under aggressive compression, while stronger query-conditioned signals become available after substantial computation within the large language model (LLM). This raises a natural question: can structurally coherent, query-aware token selection be performed before consulting the LLM? We therefore propose ST-Pruner (Spectral-Textual Pruner), a training-free framework for pre-LLM visual-token selection. It combines attention-independent spectral saliency with inverted patch-text similarity through parameter-free multiplicative fusion. Across diverse LVLMs, ST-Pruner retains over 95% of full-token performance using at most 11.1% of visual tokens and achieves a 3.2x end-to-end speedup on LLaVA-NeXT. Code is available at https://github.com/sejong-rcv/ST-Pruner.
authors: Intaek Shin, Geuntaek Lim, Sungjune Park, Yukyung Choi
bullets: LVLMs face high inference costs from long visual-token sequences.
Visual [CLS] attention can select scattered, background-biased tokens, while query-aware signals typically require costly LLM computation.
ST-Pruner is training-free and operates before LLM processing.
It fuses attention-independent spectral saliency with inverted patch-text similarity using parameter-free multiplication.
Across diverse LVLMs, it achieves a 3.2× end-to-end speedup on LLaVA-NeXT while retaining over 95% of full-token performance.

Their parameter-free multiplicative fusion determines the top-K visual tokens, which are retained in their original sequence order before LLM inference. The textual query is independently tokenized for the standard languagemodel input.

papers.abstract: Vision Transformers (ViTs) achieve strong image recognition performance, but their self-attention increases quadratically with the number of input tokens and makes them computationally expensive. The standard implementation of ViT models treats all patch tokens with equal importance across every layer of the model. This uniform treatment introduces redundant computation and may reduce the model's focus on the most discriminative object regions. In this paper, we propose ConvRoute-ViT, a convolutional token routing mechanism for efficient vision transformers that performs token reduction through convolutional routing. Our model preserves the most relevant patch tokens according to class-token attention at selected layers, while the remaining tokens are spatially reorganized and compressed into a compact set of convolutional summary tokens. This design reduces the sequence length without completely removing the contextual information of the less informative tokens. By applying the routing process hierarchically, the proposed framework constructs compact and discriminative representations for deeper layers. Experiments on CIFAR-100 and TinyImageNet show that ConvRoute-ViT improves computational efficiency while maintaining classification accuracy compared with the base ViT.
authors: Manish Das, Shiv Ram Dubey, Satish Kumar Singh
bullets: Addresses redundant computation from treating all ViT patch tokens equally and the quadratic cost of self-attention.
Uses class-token attention to preserve relevant tokens at selected layers.
Spatially reorganizes and convolves remaining tokens into compact summary tokens rather than discarding them.
Applies routing hierarchically to build compact, discriminative representations in deeper layers.
Experiments on CIFAR-100 and TinyImageNet report improved computational efficiency with maintained classification accuracy versus base ViT.

figures.caption: Fig. 1. Overview of the proposed ConvRoute-ViT architecture. The input image is converted into patch tokens with positional encoding and a CLS token, creating an input size of B×N ×D. After initial transformer processing up to kth transformer layers, the ConvRoute Token Routing Module computes the token importance score and retains the top-R important tokens. The remaining tokens are passed through the ConvRoute Compressor where they are spatially reshaped to generate compact ConvSummary tokens, resulting in B ×M ×D and are processed by transformer layers from k+1→ l. A second ConvRoute Token Routing Module is applied at layer l to further reduce the sequence and is then passed through the subsequent transformer blocks for final classification.

Fig. 2. Attention heatmaps for representative CIFAR-100 samples [24]. Each example consists of three panels arranged from left to right: the input image, the base ViT attention map, and the ConvRoute-ViT attention map.

papers.abstract: Sparse Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models offer scalable capacity for Web applications, but uneven routing creates computation and communication bottlenecks. Existing placement and replication methods redistribute this workload, yet additional expert copies compete with token-related buffers for limited GPU memory. We present LRMoE, a memory-aware MoE training system that jointly recalibrates backward demand and balances the retained workload. During forward execution, it plans retention quotas and expert placement under resource constraints while preserving all routed computations. During backpropagation, a load recalibration metric estimates each token-expert pair's contribution to the expert update and selects pairs within these quotas. A capacity-aware routing algorithm distributes retained pairs among eligible instances of their original experts. Physical compaction then forms smaller communication payloads and variable-size grouped GEMMs, reducing backward traffic, computation, and execution-buffer demand. Experiments on Qwen3-30B-A3B and GLM4.5-106B-A12B show that LRMoE reduces cumulative MoE-layer training time to fixed-loss targets by 21.2-44.8% relative to SYMI.
authors: Jiaming Hu, Zhida Jiang, Zhaolong Xing, Yu Li, Zhen Chen, Ke Zhang

Plans retention quotas and expert placement during the forward pass without dropping routed computations.
Uses backward-demand recalibration to select token–expert pairs and capacity-aware routing to distribute them across expert instances.
Compacts retained pairs into smaller communication payloads and variable-size grouped GEMMs.
On Qwen3-30B-A3B and GLM4.5-106B-A12B, reduces cumulative MoE-layer training time to fixed-loss targets by 21.2–44.8% versus SYMI.

papers.abstract: Different visual token pruning strategies retain different subsets while maintaining similar task performance. This motivates a combinatorial question: how many visual subsets can preserve model behavior, and how does their abundance depend on the query? We introduce visual sufficiency landscapes to characterize this abundance. At a fixed layer and budget, visual sufficiency probability is the fraction of uniformly sampled subsets that jointly preserve the dense model's answer, reference-answer likelihood, and output distribution. Independent sampling replicates separate input variation from estimation noise. Across Qwen2.5-VL-7B, InternVL2-8B, and LLaVA-v1.5-7B, differences between inputs on GQA and TextVQA exceed replication error, and different questions about the same GQA image produce distinct landscapes. Sufficiency probability also improves failure prediction for full pruning methods. On LLaVA, adding this probability increases AUC by 0.1151 for FastV, 0.0683 for VisionZip, and 0.1401 for SparseVLM, while reducing log loss and Brier score. Several architecture-adapted configurations on the other two models reproduce these gains. Under controlled selection rules, predictors trained on the original images reduce log loss on new images by 9.0%, 13.0%, and 14.1%, respectively. These results establish successful-subset abundance as a measurable dimension of local prunability and connect it to the identification of high-risk pruning conditions.
authors: Zhenghan Li
Kexin Sun
Wei Zheng
Peng Hu
Xiao Wei
Anbo Huang
bullets: The study asks how the abundance of behavior-preserving visual subsets varies with the query.

Across three vision-language models, landscapes differ by input and by question for the same image beyond sampling error.
Sufficiency probability improves failure prediction for FastV, VisionZip, and SparseVLM, with reported AUC gains and lower log loss and Brier scores.
The work frames successful-subset abundance as a measurable dimension of local prunability and a signal for high-risk pruning conditions.

papers.abstract: Diffusion language models offer a promising path to efficient agents through parallel token generation. However, efficient interaction requires adapting both where computation is spent and how much text is generated. We introduce a metacognitive controller that guides diffusion generation according to the needs of the current response and the agent's interaction with the environment. It learns when to finalize tokens and how far generation should extend, reducing overall computation within responses. Our controller, a lightweight plug-in for the diffusion backbone, is trained on agent trajectories to balance correctness and generation cost. This approach connects the agent's generation process to the interaction the agent serves. Experiments across five benchmarks demonstrate that our approach reduces inference FLOPs by 20.6% on average compared with the most efficient baseline, while maintaining competitive task accuracy. Ablation studies further validate the effectiveness of our approach.
authors: Mingyu Zhao, Shuhang Lin, Ligong Han, Xiaojing Yu, Zhenting Wang, Yifei Pang, Yang Zhou, Dimitris N. Metaxas
bullets: Targets the challenge of reducing computation while preserving agent response quality.
Learns when to finalize tokens and how far generation should continue.
Trained on agent trajectories to balance correctness with generation cost.
Reduces inference FLOPs by 20.6% on average across five benchmarks versus the most efficient baseline, while maintaining competitive task accuracy.
Ablation studies support the controller’s effectiveness.

Blank blue cells have no saved token text. Flux decoding reduces the active range (gray). papers.selection_reason: Adaptive token finalization and generation-length control reduce inference FLOPs for diffusion language agents, fitting efficient token-level computation.
papers.title: Metacognitive Decoding: Efficient Inference for Diffusion Language Agents
papers.tldr: A lightweight metacognitive controller makes diffusion language agents more efficient by adapting token finalization and response length to interaction needs.

papers.abstract: Current 3D scene understanding pipelines typically concatenate vast numbers of 3D object tokens with text tokens and feed the resulting sequence to a Large Language Model (LLM). However, existing 3D-LLMs for scene understanding encounter two major limitations: (i) excessive inclusion of task-irrelevant object data, introducing noise that reduces reasoning accuracy and increases hallucinations; and (ii) reliance solely on point cloud data, which inherently lacks the rich semantic information available in complementary 2D modalities, such as color, material properties, texture, and high-level contextual relationships. To address these challenges, we introduce 3D-SceneQ, a 3D LLM that unifies adaptive token pruning with multimodal semantic enrichment, markedly advancing scene understanding, reasoning, and grounding. Specifically, we propose a Query-Guided Adaptive Pruning (QGAP) module that adaptively selects task-relevant objects based on the intended meaning of user instructions, leveraging a learnable latent query to retain critical information while effectively suppressing irrelevant noise. In addition, we introduce a Multi-modal Object-level Feature Enhancement (MOFE) module, which integrates 2D feature embeddings from pre-trained models into 3D representation to enrich object-level semantic information. Evaluations show that 3D-SceneQ outperforms current state-of-the-art methods across multiple benchmarks (e.g., +5.7 CIDEr on Scan2Cap and +17.0 EM@1 on SQA3D), demonstrating its remarkable capabilities in various 3D language reasoning tasks.
authors: Yongqi Shan, Lu Zhang, Jiazuo Yu, Yunzhi Zhuge, Huchuan Lu
bullets: Addresses noise from feeding large numbers of task-irrelevant 3D object tokens to LLMs.
Uses Query-Guided Adaptive Pruning (QGAP) to retain objects relevant to the user instruction.
Uses Multi-modal Object-level Feature Enhancement (MOFE) to integrate pretrained 2D features into 3D representations.
Outperforms prior state-of-the-art methods on multiple benchmarks, including +5.7 CIDEr on Scan2Cap and +17.0 EM@1 on SQA3D.
Targets 3D scene understanding, reasoning, and grounding tasks.

papers.abstract: Pruned language models are judged almost entirely by accuracy and perplexity, which assumes that preserved output behaviour implies preserved internal computation. We test this assumption with a factorial pruning study on GPT-2, crossing two importance criteria (magnitude, random), two component types (attention heads, MLP neurons) and three sparsity levels (3%, 50%, 70%). Using the fully characterised indirect object identification (IOI) circuit as ground truth, we measure circuit integrity with activation patching, path patching and direct logit attribution. We find two qualitatively distinct failure modes. Magnitude head pruning >= zeroes the circuit: output-facing heads are removed, and the model falls to near-chance. Magnitude neuron pruning at 30% inverts it: all 26 circuit heads remain intact, but Name Mover contributions flip sign, and the model systematically prefers the wrong name (17.7% accuracy). Perplexity ranks it as less damaged than random head pruning (74.6 vs 140.1). A replication of the Greater-Than circuit shows that the critical component type depends on the circuit's architecture. These results show that output metrics and structural checks can both miss mechanistic damage, motivating circuit-level causal analysis as a complementary evaluation of compressed language models.
authors: Nabeelah Faumi, Deshan Sumanathilaka
bullets: The study tests magnitude and random pruning of GPT-2 attention heads and MLP neurons across multiple sparsity levels.
Circuit integrity is evaluated using activation patching, path patching, and direct logit attribution, with IOI as the primary ground truth.
Magnitude head pruning can remove output-facing circuit heads and reduce performance to near chance.
Magnitude neuron pruning can leave all circuit heads intact while reversing Name Mover contributions, yielding systematically wrong predictions.
A Greater-Than circuit replication shows that pruning sensitivity depends on circuit architecture; circuit-level causal analysis is therefore needed alongside perplexity and structural checks.

papers.selection_reason: Investigates mechanistic failure modes of weight pruning in Transformers using mechanistic interpretability. This provides a deeper understanding of how pruning affects internal computation, relevant to LLMs and model efficiency.
papers.title: Mechanistic Failure Modes of Weight Pruning in Transformer Language Models
papers.tldr: Weight pruning can preserve or obscure output-level performance while severely damaging the internal circuits that produce model behavior.

papers.abstract: Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) has been widely adopted for aligning language models with human preferences. Recent empirical work has revealed that DPO induces remarkably sparse parameter updates, yet no theoretical explanation for this phenomenon has been offered. We analyze DPO's optimization dynamics under a neural tangent kernel linearization and show that the logistic structure of the DPO loss gives rise to an implicit maximum-margin bias. Building on this observation, we introduce the concept of dual sparsity: the DPO update direction is a sparse linear combination (data-level sparsity, driven by support vectors) of sparse gradient feature vectors (parameter-level sparsity, arising from gradient cancellation between preferred and dispreferred responses). We formalize this structure in our main theorem, bound the number of support pairs by a margin-dependent spectral quantity, and present a framework relating dual sparsity to weight disentanglement---a condition favorable for model merging. Experiments on GPT-2 Small and Medium and on 7--9B instruction-tuned models (Llama-3-8B, Mistral-7B, Gemma-2-9B) with the Anthropic HH-RLHF and UltraFeedback datasets confirm both sources of sparsity, and experiments on GPT-2 show that DPO reduces cross-task interference by up to $35{\times}$ compared to supervised fine-tuning.
authors: Kensuke Sasaki, Issei Sato
bullets: DPO’s logistic loss creates an implicit maximum-margin optimization bias.
Its update is sparse at two levels: support-vector-like data sparsity and gradient-cancellation-driven parameter sparsity.
A theorem bounds the number of support pairs using a margin-dependent spectral quantity.
The framework connects dual sparsity with weight disentanglement, a property useful for model merging.
Experiments across GPT-2 and several 7–9B instruction-tuned models confirm both sparsity mechanisms; on GPT-2, DPO reduces cross-task interference by up to 35× versus supervised fine-tuning.

papers.selection_reason: Analyzes the sparsity of Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) updates, providing a theoretical explanation for weight disentanglement. This connects alignment (LLMs) with efficiency (sparsity) and model merging.
papers.title: On the Sparsity of Direct Preference Optimization: Weight Disentanglement in the NTK Regime
papers.tldr: DPO’s sparse parameter updates are theoretically explained by dual sparsity in the NTK regime, which also promotes weight disentanglement and reduces cross-task interference.

papers.abstract: Vision-Language Models (VLMs) have demonstrated remarkable multimodal capabilities but suffer from prohibitive computational overhead due to the massive number of visual tokens. While token pruning is a promising solution, existing methods still suffer from two major drawbacks: 1) unreliable pruning criteria that fail to accurately localize task-specific regions due to inherent attention biases or query-agnostic designs, and 2) suboptimal pruning strategies that employ rigid, non-adaptive schedules, overlooking the dynamic evolution of token redundancy across different model depths. To address these challenges, we propose LearnPrunerV2, which extends the previous two-stage heuristic framework (LearnPruner) into a fully learnable architecture. Specifically, we integrate lightweight learnable modules into every layer of the VLM backbone, which estimate token importance by fusing intrinsic visual saliency with extrinsic query relevance captured via a shadow token. By uncovering a consistent staircase redundancy pattern across VLM layers, we further introduce Budget-Deterministic Pruning (BDP) to establish a hardware-friendly schedule with fixed per-layer budgets. Extensive experimental results across various benchmarks and VLMs demonstrate that LearnPrunerV2 consistently outperform previous state-of-the-art methods. Notably, LearnPrunerV2 preserves 99.8% of the original performance when pruning 77.8% of visual tokens on LLaVA-v1.5, achieving a superior accuracy-efficiency trade-off.
authors: Rinyoichi Takezoe, Yaqian Li, Weiren Wang, Zihao Bo, Huihong Shi, Anzhou Hou, Mo Guang, Jiale Yan, Kaiwen Long
bullets: Targets excessive computation from the large number of visual tokens in VLMs.
Uses lightweight per-layer modules to estimate token importance from visual saliency and query relevance via a shadow token.
Introduces Budget-Deterministic Pruning, a fixed per-layer schedule guided by the observed staircase pattern of token redundancy.
Across benchmarks and VLMs, it reportedly outperforms prior state-of-the-art pruning methods.
On LLaVA-v1.5, it retains 99.8% of original performance while pruning 77.8% of visual tokens.

papers.abstract: Diffusion vision-language models (DVLMs) process their entire input at every denoising step. Since visual tokens make up 89-97% of this input on the benchmarks we study, most of the decoding computation is spent repeatedly processing the same image. Visual token pruning methods partially relieve this burden by removing part of the visual tokens, but they lose the removed information and still process the remaining image at every step. To measure how often the image is actually needed, we compare LLaDA-V's predictions with and without the image at every decoding step and find that removing the image changes a token being unmasked at only 22.8% of steps on average and at as few as 7.9%. We therefore propose LOWN, a decoding method that decides at every step whether to process the image and how many tokens to unmask. LOWN predicts the masked tokens without the image and processes the image only when this prediction disagrees with the last image-conditioned prediction. Agreement certifies the earlier prediction for reuse, and the number of certified tokens sets how many are unmasked in that step. We further observe that the need for the image differs across benchmarks, so LOWN's adaptive decision is needed rather than a fixed schedule. Without training or a tuned threshold, LOWN retains 99.6% of LLaDA-V's score on ten benchmarks at 35.3% of the decoding FLOPs on average. LOWN also generalizes across LLaDA-based DVLMs, composes orthogonally with visual token pruning, and runs under key-value caching for further efficiency gains. Code and project page are available at https://hyeon9698.github.io/LOWN/
authors: Donghyeon Cho, Joowon Kim, Seungho Shin, Eunho Yang
bullets: DVLMs repeatedly process mostly redundant visual tokens at every denoising step.
The method compares image-free and image-conditioned predictions to certify when prior predictions can be reused.
It adaptively decides both whether to process the image and how many tokens to unmask, without training or a tuned threshold.
Across ten benchmarks, LOWN retains 99.6% of LLaDA-V’s score while using 35.3% of the decoding FLOPs on average.
It generalizes across LLaDA-based DVLMs, combines with visual token pruning, and supports key-value caching.

papers.selection_reason: Adaptive visual routing reduces decoding FLOPs for diffusion VLMs.
papers.title: Look Only When Needed: Certificate-Guided Visual Routing for Efficient Diffusion VLMs
papers.tldr: LOWN makes diffusion VLMs process image tokens only when needed, preserving nearly all performance while substantially reducing decoding computation.

papers.abstract: Video Large Language Models (VLMs) have demonstrated strong capabilities in video understanding and reasoning, but processing long visual sequences incurs substantial computational, latency, and memory overhead. This survey examines training-free inference acceleration, focusing on reducing inference costs while preserving task-relevant spatiotemporal evidence. We organize existing methods by their intervention stages in the inference pipeline, covering input, visual encoding, projector, prefill, and decoding. Post-training quantization (PTQ) is discussed separately as a cross-stage extension with varying calibration requirements. We analyze how intervention position affects evidence preservation and computational savings, and why local efficiency improvements may not translate into end-to-end acceleration. We complement this analysis with quantitative evidence from prior studies and our own experiments under a shared evaluation setting to assess accuracy-latency trade-offs.

papers.abstract: Diffusion large language models (dLLMs) enable flexible generation through iterative masked denoising, but incur substantial inference cost because token representations are repeatedly recomputed across denoising steps. Existing cache-based methods reduce this cost by reusing intermediate results across denoising steps and recomputing only a subset of positions at each step, chosen either on a fixed schedule or by heuristic signals of change. Our trajectory experiments instead point to decoding trajectory as the more relevant quantity. Cached generation remains accurate when it stays close to the full-denoising trajectory, with errors concentrated around unmask-order deviations and reduced as longer reference prefixes are recovered. This suggests a more direct principle: limiting representation error helps, but keeping generation on the full-denoising trajectory is a more direct route to accurate decoding. We therefore formulate efficient dLLM inference as trajectory-guided querying. Rather than broadly repairing representation error, we use full-denoising trajectories to supervise which unresolved positions should receive limited fresh computation. Based on this formulation, we introduce TRACEQUERY, a lightweight sparse decoding framework that predicts a small set of near-future trajectory-relevant positions, queries only those candidates, and lets the backbone select which one to commit from their fresh predictions. TRACEQUERY delivers the strongest quality-computation trade-off among cache-based approaches, sustaining high accuracy with substantially fewer fresh token computations, and generalizes across tasks, model variants, and families. papers.abstract: Attention over tens of thousands of visual tokens dominates the inference of video diffusion transformers (DiTs). Existing methods reduce this cost through sparsity, low precision, or both, but use a single precision for all kept tiles. We observe that the output error introduced by approximation varies widely across tiles. Many tiles can be skipped with little error, others must be computed but gain little beyond low precision, and a few retain substantial error even at low precision. We present Triage, a training-free attention method that assigns each tile one of three approximation tiers: skipping it by replacing it with its block means, skimming it in NVFP4, or refining it with NVFP4 residual correction. A lightweight router predicts each tile's error under each tier from block statistics and moves a tile to a more accurate tier only when the predicted error reduction justifies the extra compute, with a single price setting this trade-off. A fused kernel executes all three tiers in a single pass on the FP4 tensor cores of RTX Blackwell GPUs. Across Wan2.2, HunyuanVideo, and LTX-2.5, Triage accelerates end-to-end generation by up to 2.32x over dense FlashAttention, and in each of five settings it runs faster than every baseline while reaching 0.3-3.0 dB higher PSNR than the highest-PSNR baseline.
authors: Yeonjae Kim, Omin Kwon, Seong Hoon Seo, Jae W. Lee
bullets: Targets the high inference cost of attention over tens of thousands of video tokens.

Across three video diffusion models and five settings, it achieves up to 2.32× end-to-end speedup and 0.3–3.0 dB higher PSNR than the strongest baseline.

papers.abstract: Deploying large vision-language models (LVLMs) on resource-constrained embodied agents for 3D visual question answering necessitates cloud-edge collaboration. However, offloading massive visual data to the cloud over bandwidth-limited and noisy channels introduces severe latency and transmission distortion. To address this, we propose TP-JSCC, an efficient token pruning and joint source-channel coding method for LVLMs-based 3D-VQA in Cloud-Edge Collaboration. First, we develop a Local and Global Semantics-based Hybrid Token Pruning (LGS-HTP) module to significantly reduce the visual token count. By decoupling foreground-background tokens and jointly selecting local and global semantics, LGS-HTP effectively reduces redundancy while preserving reasoning-critical tokens. Second, we introduce a lightweight Token Joint Source-Channel Coding (T-JSCC) module to further compress the pruned tokens and ensure their robust transmission over error-prone channels. By employing lightweight cascaded linear layers and Signal-to-Noise Ratio (SNR)-adaptive mechanism, this module adapts to fluctuating channel conditions while maintaining minimal computational overhead. Extensive experiments on ScanQA and SQA3D datasets indicate the exceptional efficiency and robustness of our approach. Specifically, on ScanQA validation set, the LGS-HTP module could achieve 90% pruning ratio while incurring less than a 1% CIDEr loss. Building on this, the T-JSCC further compresses the tokens by 18 times, resulting in an overall 180 times data volume reduction for robust transmission, while saving 90% in computational complexity for LVLM deployment. Our code is available at https://github.com/yuanhui0325/TP-JSCC.
authors: Zhengxin Li, Chongzhen Tian, Hui Yuan, Hao Liu, Sam Kwong
